## DL-323 — the writeback resolves a card id THROUGH the mapped board, not against it: a foreign card id is now refused by a board-scoped check before any unscoped read (card#8375)

**Status:** implemented (card#8375). No migration, no new config key, no `.env` change, no token-scope change. ⚠ **CHANGES WHAT THE WRITEBACK ACCEPTS — see the accept/reject section below.** One additional kanban read per `kanban_move_card` delivery.

**Context.** `payload.card_id` reaches `KanbanMoveCardHandler` as a literal integer parsed out of **author-controlled text** — a `card#NNNN` token in a PR title or head ref (`CardTokenGrammar`) — and kanban's card id space is **GLOBAL across every board on the instance**. The handler resolved it with `KanbanClient::getCard()`, i.e. `GET /tasks/{id}.json`, an endpoint that names **no board**, and only afterwards compared the returned `board_id` against the mapping (DL-009 / DL-292). So the tenant boundary's precondition was *a successful cross-tenant read*, and on a 403 the compare was not reached at all — the read threw first (DL-314 recorded that the 403 arm is the operator's only signal there, and that a board-scoped read was the thing that could have decided it). **Measured live on a shared instance:** a repo event on one install resolved to a card id another install owns. It failed closed — but only because the API answered 403, i.e. because of what that token's scope happened to be. Nothing asserted the scope stays narrow and **no test went red if it widened**, which by this repo's own standard (a guarantee with no check is a comment, not a contract) is the defect. The remaining half of roundtable #379; the disclosure half shipped at DL-314 and is deliberately not redone here.

- **⚑ Decision 1 — ask the SERVER for `(board, id)` before reading the card.** New `KanbanClient::cardRowsOnBoard($boardId, $cardId, $archivedOnly)` issues `GET /tasks/search.json?q=board_id=<mapped> id=<card>&limit=1`, both terms **inside `q=`** per the DL-298/card#7211 invariant. `id=<digits>` is a `QueryParser` structured filter (`where('id','=',N)`) that has existed since kanban's first commit. `MappedBoardGuard::refusesCardIdOutsideMappedBoard()` runs it **immediately after the client is built and before `getCard()`**, so an id outside the mapping is never resolved at all rather than being resolved and refused downstream.

- **⛔ Decision 2 — the verdict is read off the ROWS, never off the call.** The same endpoint drops an unrecognised top-level parameter in silence and answers 200, and an unrecognised `q` term degrades to free text; nothing in a 200 distinguishes a scoped read from an unscoped one (rt#327). A row therefore establishes membership only if its own `id` names the card **and** `MappedBoardGuard::belongs()` accepts its own `board_id` — the same predicate, and the same rule DL-298 applies to search-resolved write rows. A consequence worth stating: a server that stopped honouring `id=` cannot produce a false ACCEPT, only a refusal, and that refusal has its own reason rather than being reported as a tenant verdict.

- **⚑ Decision 3 — BOTH sides of the archive switch, so nothing narrows silently.** kanban's search excludes archived rows unless `?archived` is passed and offers no both-sides mode (DL-296). A live-only check would have started refusing every archived card on the mapped board — a second accept/reject change riding along on this one, and one nobody asked for. The archived probe therefore runs **only when the live side misses**: the happy path is one request, the refusal path three.

- **⭐ Decision 4 — THREE refusal reasons, discriminated by a CONTROL rather than by inference.** DL-314 recorded that a 403 cannot choose between *a foreign card id* and *this token's own scope*. An empty board-scoped answer has the same ambiguity, so after a miss the mapped board is probed on its own (`visibility()`): `card_id_outside_mapped_board` is claimed only when the board that would carry the card reads back; otherwise the weaker `mapped_board_unreadable_to_this_token`, whose text says an unreadable board and a genuinely empty one are one answer here. A lookup that answered somebody else's row is `board_scope_lookup_unfiltered` — a broken read, explicitly not a tenant verdict. The control never changes WHETHER the move is refused, only which reason, so its own failure degrades to the weaker verdict instead of propagating.

- **⚑ Decision 5 — the transient/permanent split is unchanged, and applies to the new read.** A 5xx/timeout on the scope lookup **throws** (→ 5xx → redelivery); a 4xx is a permanent refusal (alert + log + no-op), because a 5xx on a body that fails identically every time is the DL-020 storm. All four arms **withhold the card id from the alert channel** (DL-314) and keep it in the `Log::warning` — this is the case that rule was written for.

- **⭐ Decision 6 — `getCard`'s 403 slug is NARROWED on this arm, because the hypothesis it names is now excluded by a measurement.** `RefusalContext::readReason()` gains `bool $foreignIdExcluded`; `kanban_move_card` passes it and emits `getcard_403_token_scope`. By the time that arm fires, the same token has read this id back off the mapped board, so *foreign card id* is not a live cause and naming it would send the operator hunting a card that is demonstrably theirs. **`kanban_block_reason` makes no such check and keeps `getcard_403_foreign_card_id_or_token_scope`**, which is still the honest answer there — pinned by a new leg in its own test class so the difference cannot rot into an unexplained inconsistency.

- **⚠ ACCEPT/REJECT — what changes.** **Newly REFUSED:** a `kanban_move_card` delivery whose `card_id` does not resolve on the repo's mapped board. On a correctly-scoped install that set is **empty by construction** — every card the writeback legitimately moves is on the mapped board, or the post-read DL-009 guard was already refusing it. What moves is *where* it is refused (before the read, not after) and *whether the refusal survives a widened token* (it does now). **Newly refused for a real reason, and this is the operator-visible cost:** an install whose writeback token cannot READ its own mapped board through `/tasks/search.json` now refuses every move under `mapped_board_unreadable_to_this_token` instead of proceeding via the unscoped read — that install was one token-scope change away from cross-tenant writes, and `bridge:check`'s visibility probe already reports it at preflight. **UNCHANGED:** every move on a correctly-scoped install, the archived-card population (Decision 3), the pin / no-regression / corroboration guards, the alert body shape, the dedup tuple, and both the post-read `MappedBoardGuard::refuses()` compare and its divergence ledger.

- **Alternatives considered:**
  - **Keep the unscoped read and rely on the post-read compare.** Rejected — that IS the current state, and it is what the card was filed on: the compare's precondition is the cross-tenant read, it is structurally unreachable on a 403, and the alert path on the token arm can echo an unestablished id.
  - **Replace `getCard()` with the search row entirely (one read, not two).** Rejected: the search row is a `TaskResource` collection member and does not carry `comments`, which the card#7064 note dedup reads off the card aggregate; and `last_stage_move` / payload assumptions across the handler are written against the full aggregate. Cheaper by one request, paid for in a semantic change nobody costed.
  - **Gate the scope check on the resolution route (skip it for by-ref-resolved ids, which are already board-scoped).** Rejected: it puts a second, quieter accept path into the security boundary and makes the guard's correctness depend on the classifier stamping provenance the handler cannot verify — the shape DL-266 and card#7211 both argue against. One request is not worth a conditional boundary.
  - **Add a `bridge:check` leg instead of a runtime check.** Rejected as an answer to this card: preflight reports a state, it does not refuse a delivery. Complementary, not a substitute.

- **Consequences:** `app/Bridge/Writeback/KanbanClient.php` (+`cardRowsOnBoard`, `getCard`'s docblock now states its unscoped-ness and names its precondition); `app/Bridge/Writeback/MappedBoardGuard.php` (+`refusesCardIdOutsideMappedBoard`, +3 reason constants, +2 private helpers — the class now owns both entry points to one rule); `app/Bridge/Handlers/KanbanMoveCardHandler.php` (the check, and the 403 arm's message + narrowed slug); `app/Bridge/Support/RefusalContext.php` (`readReason`'s `$foreignIdExcluded`); `app/Bridge/Handlers/KanbanBlockReasonHandler.php` (comment only — records that the two arms are no longer twins on the 403 and why); `app/Bridge/Classifiers/GitHubPrCardMoveClassifier.php` (comment only — its enumeration of what the durable handler refuses gained the new first refusal). New `tests/Feature/Writeback/WritebackTenantScopeTest.php` (8 legs; 7 red without the check) and `tests/Support/ScopeLookupStub.php`; `BoardScopedReadConstructionTest` floors +1 read and +1 call site; `RefusalContextTest` +1; `KanbanBlockReasonHandlerTest` +1; `KanbanMoveCardHandlerTest` (the fallback stub, two slug pins, and one leg REVERSED — see below). Docs: `docs/writeback.md` (a section, 6 table rows, the `card_id_withheld` paragraph), `docs/kanban-integration-contract.md` (a new §2 row for the scoped read + the unscoped-read row's warning), `docs/CHANGELOG.md`.

- **⚠ ONE EXISTING TEST'S CLAIM WAS REVERSED, deliberately and in the open.** `test_getcard_403_log_names_both_hypotheses` required the move handler's 403 text to offer BOTH causes (DL-314). It now asserts the opposite for that arm — that the text says the foreign-card-id cause is EXCLUDED — because a message still offering both would send the operator after a cause this arm can no longer have. The two-cause wording is not retired: it moved to `KanbanBlockReasonHandlerTest`, where it is still true, so deleting it here does not retire the assertion that it exists somewhere.

- **Bounds, stated.** **NOT MEASURED AGAINST A LIVE KANBAN.** The `id=` term is **source-verified** — read out of `app/Services/TaskSearch/QueryParser.php` in the sibling repo, present since its first commit — not exercised against a running instance with a control the way `q=board_id=` was at rt#327. That is the weaker evidence, and it is why Decision 2 refuses to trust the call: the failure direction of a wrong reading is refusal, not admission. **`kanban_block_reason` IS THE SAME DEFECT SHAPE AND IS NOT FIXED HERE** — its card id comes from the same token grammar against the same global id space, and its `getCard` is equally unscoped; the overlay writes one field and never moves a card, but that is a smaller blast radius, not a different class. Filed as **card#8415**, and disclosed in the handler, in `readReason()`'s docblock and in `docs/writeback.md` rather than left to be inferred. **`kanban_coord_card_move` is NOT in the class**: its ids come from `cardsByTag`/`correlateIssue`, both board-scoped, and its rows already re-check through the same guard. **TWO SMALLER POPULATIONS NARROW WITH IT, found in review and disclosed rather than chased.** (1) **A SOFT-DELETED card on the mapped board.** `GET /tasks/{id}.json` is routed `->withTrashed()`, so it returns a trashed card and the old path would move it; `/tasks/search.json` applies the SoftDeletes scope and does not, so such an id is now refused. Reaching it would mean widening `BoardScopedReadConstructionTest::SEARCH_SWITCHES` with `trashed` — a claim about the server that this change cannot measure live — to preserve the ability to move a card somebody deleted. Ruled not worth it: the refusal is loud, and a deleted card is not a move target. (2) **A writeback token whose user is a SUPER-ADMIN but not a MEMBER of the mapped board.** kanban's search deliberately scopes to `Board::visibleTo($user)` — explicit membership/ownership, never super-admin mode — while `show` authorises through the `view` policy, so such a token could read the card and cannot search the board, and every move now refuses under `mapped_board_unreadable_to_this_token`. That install is already reported broken at preflight: `bridge:check`'s visibility probe reads the SAME endpoint and warns on 0 cards (DL-026), and the refusal message points at exactly that. Both are recorded here and in `docs/CHANGELOG.md`, not silently absorbed. **The extra request is per delivery, not per card**: a bundled PR moving N cards makes N scoped lookups (each names a different id, so there is nothing to memoise), against 1 preload and N card reads today.

## DL-327 — the writeback honours `[no-close]` on the PR title: the one refusal no predicate over the artifact can derive, expressed as a SUBTRACTION on the marker CI already accepts (card#8344)

- **Date:** 2026-09-01
- **Status:** implemented (card#8344, roundtable 388 origin — the shape is aimla-pm's ask: *"a `bypass`-style opt-out ON THE PR that the RUNTIME reads … it puts the authority where the authority actually is, costs nothing on the common path, and needs no author to rename anything"*). **⚠ CHANGES WHAT THE WRITEBACK ACTS ON** — the always-ask class, operator-approved before any code. No migration, no new config key, no `.env` change, no token-scope change, no receiver accept/reject change, and **no CI accept-set change** (`pr-title-lint` already accepted this marker and its verdicts are byte-unchanged). Operator-visible: a merged PR whose title carries `[no-close]` stops moving the card it cites, and both withheld-move lines say so in their own words.
- **The number:** allocated with `python3 bin/decision-log.py next` (DL-295), not derived from this file.

**The defect, and it is the LAST of four doors into the same terminal move.** Since DL-308 a merge closes a card **structurally** whenever the head ref names it — which is exactly what `board-card-start` mints. A PR written *for* a card while deliberately **not finishing** it (a design note, a reference doc, a partial spike on the card's branch) carries **precisely that ref**, so merging it promoted the card into a terminal stage, asserting work landed that did not. Measured twice on real merges: `mezzanine#24` → card 7341 (roundtable 388, reported by aimla-pm) and the same shape again inside card#7348's population. **Under-promotion is recoverable by hand; this direction is not** — the release sweep then propagates it into Released.

**⛔ WHY NO PREDICATE COULD HAVE CLOSED IT, which is what separates this from the three doors already shut.** card#8294 (the strict token), card#8306 / DL-318 (the revert) and card#8289 (`PinGuard` on every outcome) each answer a question about the **artifact** — the ref's spelling, GitHub's wrappers, the card's own markers. *"I am citing this card, not closing it"* is a fact about the **author's intent**, and a context PR is, on the branch and in the diff, **indistinguishable** from the PR that finishes the card. There is nothing to read. The only place the answer can come from is the person who already knows it.

**⛔ AND WHY THE CARD-SIDE PIN DOES NOT COVER IT** — the question roundtable 388 actually asked. `PinGuard` is **pre-emptive** and lives on the **card**: it helps only where somebody knew, *in advance*, that some future PR would cite that card without closing it. In the measured incident nobody did, and it was caught weeks later. (The pin's own gap is separately closed — card#8289 / PR 609, released **v0.79.0** — and that fix is real; it is simply a different mechanism for a different moment.)

**Decision — READ THE MARKER CI ALREADY ACCEPTS, and mint no second vocabulary.**

**1. `NoCloseGrammar` (new, `app/Bridge/Support`)** owns the literal `[no-close]` and the one question `marks(string $title): bool`, plus `describeRefusal()` — the sentence both operator-facing surfaces render (the DL-239 discipline, as `RevertGrammar` does for its own case). The marker is **card#8294's, unchanged**: it already exists, is already documented in `CLAUDE_CONVENTIONS.md` § *PR titles*, and already means exactly this proposition to the humans who write it — it was simply read by CI alone. A runtime-only spelling beside it would leave **two markers for one intent**, which is the divergence DL-239 keeps being re-derived to prevent.

**2. Both closure authorities consult it, and neither consumer spells it** — the DL-305 §6 / DL-308 lockstep, applied for the third time. `ClosureGrammar::remainders()` (the single choke point) returns the **empty** set when the marker is present, so `closedCardIds()`, `closedDls()` and everything derived from them refuse together; `PrOutcome::mergeClosesCard()` gains `! NoCloseGrammar::marks($title)` as a **conjunct**. The event path and `bridge:reconcile` therefore get the ruling from the same place and cannot disagree — without which `--fix` would re-plan an hour later, with a CLI's name on it, exactly the move the classifier declined.

**3. It is read off the EVENT PAYLOAD'S TITLE, never fetched.** The `pull_request` webhook already carries `pull_request.title`; the backstop already projects it through `GitHubReadClient::getPull()`. No new API call, no new token scope, and the marker is evaluated on precisely the field both paths already read.

**4. ⛔ IT SUBTRACTS; IT NEVER ADDS — and that, not the spelling, is why this is not the accept-surface DL-318 refused.** That entry declined a `[close-anyway]` marker because its effect would be to **MOVE** a card the writeback had otherwise refused to move: the first title DIRECTIVE the writeback obeys, a title's author reaching into a terminal stage. `[no-close]`'s only possible effect is to **WITHHOLD** a move. It can never select a card, authorize a stage, overturn a guard, or make the writeback act on anything it would have ignored — a term in a conjunction on one route and an early return on the other, asserted as a property over a corpus in `NoCloseGrammarTest` rather than argued in prose. So an author who writes it, **and an attacker who plants it**, can only ever cause the recoverable direction: a card that stands still, loudly warned.

**5. A LITERAL, NOT A GRAMMAR** (card#8294's ruling, inherited rather than re-decided). `no close intended`, `does not close this card`, `[noclose]` and `(no-close)` are prose and close the card exactly as before; case is free and position is free. A fuzzier surface would resume the guessing at intent this whole area exists to stop.

**6. A QUOTATION IS NOT AN ASSERTION** — DL-318's ruling **re-derived** on the second marker rather than assumed by analogy, because the case is reachable and the two readings differ. `marks()` reads the title with GitHub's quoted revert wrapper subtracted, so `[no-close]` inside `Revert "…"` is the ORIGINAL author's declaration about the ORIGINAL PR and does **not** veto a closing form this author wrote outside the quotes. A revert takes no structural route at all, so the two readings can only differ on the **lexical** one — which is exactly where DL-318's positional escape hatch lives.

**7. Both operator-facing lines name the marker as the reason**, for the same reason card#8306 minted its own sentence: the default one is **FALSE** about a marked PR. It asserts *the head branch ref does not name the card and the title carries no closing form* — untrue of a `[no-close]` PR, whose branch is normally the card's own. An operator reading that line would rename a branch to undo a refusal they deliberately requested. The marker arm is asked **first** on both surfaces; the only fixture where it and the revert arm are both true is a hand-made revert whose author typed the marker outside the quotes, where their own declaration is the answer they need.

**8. ⭐ PRECEDENCE WITH `PinGuard`: BOTH HOLD, NEITHER OVERRIDES.** They answer different questions on different surfaces at different moments, and there is **no order in which two withholdings disagree**. `[no-close]` is read at **classify** time off the event payload's title, and its refusal is strictly **earlier** — no `kanban_move_card` target is emitted at all, so the handler where `PinGuard` lives is never reached and the card's pin state cannot matter. The pin is read at **write** time off the card, on every outcome (card#8289). Either alone withholds the move; the marker cannot lift a pin (it can only withhold) and a pin cannot overrule the marker (there is nothing left to refuse). Both are stated on `NoCloseGrammar::describeRefusal()`, which is where an operator meets the question.

**9. CORRELATION IS UNTOUCHED**, exactly as for a revert. The card is still selected, `opened` / `started` / `closed_unmerged` still fire, the PR refs are still stamped, and `bridge:reconcile` keeps the card in its population — so a marker written in error is undone by deleting it, not by hunting a lost correlation.

**10. ONE LITERAL, TWO ENGINES, GUARDED.** `.github/workflows/pr-title-lint.yml`'s `optout=` cannot read a PHP constant, so `PrTitleLintTest` ties it to `NoCloseGrammar::MARKER` — the string AND the **answer sets**, comparing the step's real `tr | grep -F` against `marks()` over a corpus that splits. The workflow comment asserting *"nothing at runtime reads it"* is corrected in place; it was true when written and is the claim this decision falsifies.

- **Alternatives considered:**
  - **Mint a new runtime-only marker (`[bridge-no-move]`, a `bypass:` prefix).** Rejected — two markers for one intent, which is DL-239's defect in its purest form: an author would write one, CI would honour the other, and the divergence would be silent in the direction that PROMOTES.
  - **A branch-naming convention (*"don't call the branch `card-7341-design-ref`"*).** Rejected, and the argument is aimla-pm's, adopted rather than re-litigated: it is a rule with no check, pointed against the most natural name, defending a mechanism its authors cannot see — and it would break everything else keyed on the branch, including `pr-title-lint`'s own wider branch predicate.
  - **Rely on the card-side pin alone (card#8289).** Rejected — see above: pre-emptive, on the wrong artifact, at the wrong moment. It stays as the complementary half, not a substitute.
  - **Read a PR LABEL or the PR BODY instead of the title.** Rejected: neither is on the surface both paths already read. A label arrives on its own event (`labeled`) with no merge to gate, is mutable after merge, and would need a fetch on the backstop; the body is large, author-controlled prose in which a literal marker is far easier to plant unnoticed than in a one-line title everybody reviews. The title is also where the CI opt-out already lives, which is the whole point of reusing it.
  - **Suppress at the HANDLER instead (a payload flag from the classifier).** Rejected — the refusal would then be spelled at a third site, and `bridge:reconcile` does not pass through the handler at all, so the backstop would re-plan the move. The term belongs in the two authorities both paths already share.
  - **Do nothing; keep correcting cards by hand.** Rejected on the measured cost: the terminal move is what the release sweep propagates, it was caught weeks late once already, and the correction is manual every time.

- **Consequences:** `app/Bridge/Support/NoCloseGrammar.php` (new); `app/Bridge/Support/ClosureGrammar.php` (the veto at the choke point); `app/Bridge/Writeback/PrOutcome.php` (the conjunct, and both `describeClosure*()` sentences gain the subtractive clause — a sentence naming two routes while omitting the condition that empties both is false on the surface an operator consults to find out why nothing moved); `app/Bridge/Classifiers/GitHubPrCardMoveClassifier.php` and `app/Console/Commands/Bridge/ReconcileCommand.php` (the marker arm on each withheld-move line, three-way now); `app/Bridge/Support/RevertGrammar.php` (its *"CI-only suppression"* clause superseded, the `[close-anyway]` ruling untouched); `.github/workflows/pr-title-lint.yml` (comment corrected, skip line restated, exit-1 remediation message corrected — review R3); `CLAUDE_CONVENTIONS.md` § *PR titles* and `docs/writeback.md` § *Mention vs closure*. ⚠ **THE STALE CLAIM IS SWEPT BY PATTERN, NOT BY FILE LIST, and no count is stated here** — review R1 swept the files it had already named and left the copy with the most traffic (the step's exit-1 message) standing, so the sweep is re-derivable instead: `grep -rniE 'nothing at runtime|suppresses (this|THIS) check|CI-only|inert at runtime|no part of the bridge' --include='*.php' --include='*.md' --include='*.yml' --include='*.sh'`, cross-read against every `[no-close]` mention, with each hit either corrected or dispositioned — the two RELEASED `docs/CHANGELOG.md` rows that assert it (v0.80.0's DL-318 row, v0.79.0's card#8294 row) keep their text, which was true at release, and gain a one-clause `[superseded by DL-327]` pointer. Corrected where they stood: the three above, plus `docs/config-schema.md`'s `writeback.json` row and `docs/kanban-integration-contract.md` § *the writeback seam*, each of which enumerated the two closure routes as a COMPLETE sufficient condition, which the marker falsifies on both. Neither is re-synced: both are **shrunk to one sentence and a pointer** at `docs/writeback.md` § *Mention vs closure*, which is left as the single prose owner of the route list (canon #16 — a hand copy is what went stale here, so the repair is DELETE-and-POINT rather than one more copy that agrees today). The one copy that stays inline is `.github/workflows/pr-title-lint.yml`'s bash, which a program loads and which cannot follow a pointer — GUARDED, not deleted, by `PrTitleLintTest`'s answer-set ties (§10). ⚠ **One of them is a TEST docblock, and it was false BEFORE this decision:** `PrTitleLintTest`'s whole-step tie stated its biconditional held over *"the only [predicate] a title and a branch can decide"*, which card#8306 had already falsified — a quoted-revert title on an ORDINARY branch (outside the step's `revert-*` exemption) passes the gate and is refused by the writeback. Measured, not reasoned: `Revert "feat: widget rework (closes card#4811)"` / `fix/streaming-timeout` → step rc 0, `ClosureGrammar::closesCard()` false. Both disagreement families — the revert and this marker — are now pinned in one leg with one-variable controls, and each was watched RED (drop the `optout=` short-circuit; drop the `! NoCloseGrammar::marks()` conjunct; drop the quoted-revert subtraction). ⭐ What survives as a property is the DIRECTION, stated at the strength it holds and MEASURED rather than asserted: every disagreement that either grammar's own RULING creates — the marker, the revert — has the GATE passing and the WRITEBACK withholding, which fails toward under-promotion. ⛔ **The reverse is not unknown, it is PRICED:** DL-272's enumerated separator class (`closes<TAB|VT|FF|CR>card#N`) reds the gate on a merge the writeback would move — pinned at `PrTitleLintTest::test_the_enumerated_separator_answers_the_same_in_every_locale()`, and only TAB can reach a one-line title. Both directions, each family with its one-variable control, are enumerated and driven through the REAL extracted bash step and the REAL predicates by `PrTitleLintTest::test_the_enumerated_disagreement_families_point_the_direction_they_declare()`, which fails with the row printed on any row answering other than the direction its family declares — so a new disagreement family has to be measured there rather than written into a sentence here. Tests: `NoCloseGrammarTest` (new), plus legs on `GitHubPrCardMoveClassifierTest`, `ReconcileCommandTest`, `PrTitleLintTest` and `ReleaseTagGateTest` (the cross-repo route below) — **every witness paired with a one-variable control**, because a veto is trivially satisfied by a predicate that refuses everything, which is the DL-305 failure mode this area was built out of.

- **Bounds, stated.** **NOT MEASURED AGAINST A LIVE GITHUB DELIVERY** — the witnesses run through the shipped classifier and the shipped backstop over payload fixtures, and each was watched RED before the wiring landed and GREEN after. The incidents that motivated it were measured on real merges by their reporters, not re-measured here. ⚠ **ONE DISCLOSED DIVERGENCE, filed rather than repaired, and it is the same shape the branch and revert predicates already record:** `pr-title-lint` tests the RAW folded title for the marker while `NoCloseGrammar` subtracts the quoted revert wrapper first, so a hand-made revert QUOTING a marked title is *marked* to CI and *un-marked* to the writeback. CI then DEMANDS nothing, which is the direction that cannot produce a wrong move, and is what the `revert-*` exemption already does for GitHub's own mint. ⚠ **A title that merely MENTIONS the marker is MARKED by it**, and there is no escape hatch — a literal has no quoting rule, so a docs PR whose subject is this feature (including the PR that shipped it) declares a non-closure by talking about one. Disclosed rather than repaired: the cure is a position or context rule, which is the grammar §5 deliberately refuses, and the failure direction is under-promotion — loud, logged, fixed by moving the card. ⚠ **The marker is unauthenticated by construction** — anyone who can open a PR can write it — which is acceptable only because of §4: the worst a planted marker achieves is a card that does not move, loudly logged. ⛔ **THE GUARANTEE IS BOUNDED TO THE WRITEBACK, AND THIS REPO HAS A SECOND, CROSS-REPO ROUTE INTO THE SAME TERMINAL MOVE THAT THE MARKER DOES NOT REACH.** `.github/workflows/release-promote-cards.yml` hands the SHA-pinned `PupFuzz/agent-board-toolkit/promote` action this release's DLs, and that tool promotes a DL/PR-matched card to Released **from whatever stage it is in** unless the optional `shipped-stage-ids` input narrows it. A marked PR's card never reaches Shipped — that is what §2 withholds — so **the single conjunct standing between a `[no-close]` card and Released on the release push is `shipped-stage-ids: '52'` at that call site**, a value in a workflow, consumed by another repo's code, that no bridge predicate and no `writeback.json` can see. ⚠ **Its EQUALITY with the mapping's `stages.merged` is DECLARED HERE AND CHECKED NOWHERE:** the mapping lives in the operator's config outside this repo, so nothing in this tree can read the other side of that pair. What IS checked is the shape whose loss is the whole failure — `ReleaseTagGateTest::test_the_promote_step_pins_the_shipped_source_stage()` reds if the input is removed, blanked, or made non-numeric — all three mutations watched RED, because a deleted guard is silent and green on every surface this repo owns. An install that adopts this workflow with its own board must set its own Shipped stage id there; a mismatch skips every card instead, which is the recoverable direction.

- **Review rounds 1–2, and what the third round changed (2026-09-02).** Must-fix trend **R1=2 → R2=2**, and the **non-convergence observable fired**: each round's fix replaced one hand-written UNIVERSAL about gate/predicate disagreements with another, and a sibling leg in the same test file falsified each in turn — R1's *"the only predicate a title and a branch can decide"* by the revert family, R2's *"every known disagreement is gate-PASSES / writeback-REFUSES"* by DL-272's enumerated separator class, pinned in a sibling leg of the very file whose docblock denied it. The defect class is **a claim about a SET, held in prose over a population nobody enumerated** — each individual correction was true of what it examined and false of the set it quantified over. ⛔ The R3 resolution is therefore not a better sentence: the set is **enumerated and the direction MEASURED** (`PrTitleLintTest::test_the_enumerated_disagreement_families_point_the_direction_they_declare()`, 48 rows over 5 families through the real bash step and the real predicates), the docblocks became POINTERS to it, and the exit-1 remediation message — the highest-traffic copy of the marker's meaning and the one R1's file-scoped sweep missed — gained a test that reads it (`test_the_remediation_message_states_what_the_marker_now_does()`, a presence witness beside the absence assertion so silence cannot pass it). Both were watched RED: a row declaring the TAB case direction-1, and the superseded string restored.

## DL-324 — a CI doc-fence lint ships as a labelled BACKSTOP under DL-321's rule, reversing DL-321's decline on an operator ruling and on a measured population (card#8351)

**Status:** implemented (card#8351). ⚠ **This changes what CI REJECTS** — a new always-running workflow, `doc-fence secret backstop`, fails a PR whose markdown shell fences resolve a secret VALUE onto a readable surface. No app code, no config key, no migration, no receiver accept/reject change, no token-scope change. ⛔ **It is NOT a required status check, and an earlier draft of this line said it was.** `dev` branch protection carries nine contexts and this job's — `shell fences in *.md resolve no secret VALUE`, the JOB name, not the workflow's — is not among them (`gh api repos/…/branches/dev/protection --jq '.required_status_checks.contexts'`, read 2026-09-01). The posture is DL-295's, by name rather than re-argued: it is **not a required status check until an operator adds it to branch protection; until then it reds visibly but does not physically block a merge**. Adding it is a branch-protection config op, which is operator-gated and is deliberately **not** performed by the PR that ships this — see Consequences.

**Context.** DL-321 fixed four runbook sites, DL-322 fixed the fifth, and both entries closed on the same sentence: **nothing enforces this**. `docs/config-schema.md` § *Handling a secret VALUE (not just its file)* owns the rule and the sites link to it, so a future author has somewhere to look — and a future runbook could still mint instance six with no check anywhere reading it. card#8351 stayed open on exactly that, holding for an operator ruling on the controls that would close it.

- **⚑ Decision — build the lint DL-321 declined, and ship it as an explicitly-labelled BACKSTOP, never as the rule.** `bin/check-doc-secret-fences.py` (stdlib-only, like every other tool in `bin/`) parses the shell code fences of every `*.md` and reports a secret VALUE reaching one of the four surfaces the rule names. `.github/workflows/doc-secret-fence-lint.yml` runs it on every PR and on pushes to `dev`/`main`.

- **⛔ DL-321'S OBJECTION IS CORRECT AND IS NOT OVERTURNED HERE.** That entry declined this lint because *"a grep over spellings is the enumeration this entry rejects — it would green on the instrument nobody listed."* That is true, it is still true, and this entry does not argue otherwise. What changed is a **measurement**, not the argument: every one of the five known members of the class sat inside a markdown shell fence and **none** was in code, so a fence lint has a **5/5 catch rate on the population that has actually occurred**. The operator's ruling is that a backstop with that catch rate beats a rule with no enforcement — not that a spelling list can decide the question. ⇒ **The rule stays where DL-321 put it**, stated over the SURFACE, and this program is a net underneath it. Every artifact says so: the tool's header, its `--help` epilog, **its output on clean runs as well as dirty ones**, the workflow header, the CHANGELOG line, and this entry. A backstop that presented itself as the authority would re-mint precisely what DL-321 warned about — a reader concluding *"CI is green, therefore the class is absent"* — which is the failure this whole card exists to prevent, arriving through the fix.

- **⛔ Measured 5/5, and the denominator is stated — by an instrument that ships, not by a figure retyped from a session.** `bin/doc-fence-census.py` runs the checker over every `*.md` at every tag and prints the four numbers this entry quotes; its output, verbatim, is the source of them:

  ```text
  doc-fence-census: 85 tags / 1973 tag-file pairs / 399 findings / 5 distinct messages.
  ```

  ⚠ **An earlier draft of this entry said "1,776 markdown files … all 55 tags" and was wrong in both factors** — 55 was the unit-test COUNT leaking into the tag count (`git tag | wc -l` is 85), and 1,776 was the pair count under it. The census is why that is now checkable: it is not a CI job (a depth-1 checkout has no tags and would measure an empty history while exiting 0 — the arm it reports instead of counting), it is an operator instrument run when a figure is quoted. Every one of the five distinct messages is a known member: DL-322's `openssl dgst -hmac "$SECRET"` argv leak, DL-321's `echo "Save this token securely: …"`, its `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer …"`, and the two command-line-literal placements in `docs/provider-adapters.md` and `docs/writeback.md`. **Zero findings anywhere else, in any file, at any tag** — that is the false-positive measurement, not an impression of one. On `dev` at the time of writing: **0 findings over 29 files.**

- **⛔ ONE KNOWN MEMBER IS OUT OF REACH, AND THE 5/5 IS QUALIFIED BY IT.** DL-321's **third** site — the 401 row of `docs/multi-host.md`'s failure-mode table, *"Compare both values"* — was **prose in a markdown table**, not a fence. It is a real member of the class and this program cannot see it. So the honest claim is *5 of the 5 FENCE-RESIDENT members*, out of **six** known instances. Read the catch rate as bounded by the surface it reads, which is the same bound the rule states about instruments.

- **⚑ Fenced-executable vs. explanatory prose is the constraint the design turns on.** This repo **documents** the defect: `CLAUDE_DEPLOYMENT.md`'s smoke-test preamble quotes the argv leak in order to teach why it was wrong, and DL-321, DL-322 and `docs/CHANGELOG.md` quote several more. **A lint that reddened on the documentation of a defect is worse than no lint** — what gets deleted is the explanation. Only fences whose info string names a shell are parsed; **inline backticks in prose are never read at all**, and neither is a `text`/`json`/`php` fence. `ProseIsNeverRead` pins the discriminator on ONE payload in both directions: the same bytes are clean in backticks and red in a fence.

- **⚑ The vocabulary is derived from the rule, and the hardest half of it is the NEGATIVE half.** The four surfaces come from `docs/config-schema.md`; so do the sanctioned forms, and each is a regression case. What a naive grep gets wrong is not the leaks, it is the **prescribed** shapes that mention a secret: `printf '%s' "$SECRET" > <path>` (a builtin, so no argv), `printf … | curl --config -` (stdin, not argv), `export BRIDGE_CHANNEL_TOKEN="$(cat "$TOKEN_FILE")"` (a value into a variable, never onto stdout), `mkdir -p "$(dirname "$TOKEN_FILE")"` (a name ending in `_FILE` is a PATH, not a value), and `${VAR:+set}` (substitutes the alternative, never the value). Reddening on any of those would push an author back to the leaking spelling, so each is a named test. **Two were live defects found by those tests rather than by reading**: `${SECRET:+set}` — the exact form the rule prescribes for testing — was reported as a stdout leak, and the passthrough-tail case sat behind an `elif` it could never reach because `tee` is also a reader. A rule that cannot fire is the shape this card is about, met inside the fix for it.

- **⛔ ONE LEG IS DENY-BY-DEFAULT, WHICH MOVES THE DISCLOSED BOUND — and it was a review finding, not a design.** As first written, the pipeline-TAIL rule enumerated the tails that LEAK (`cat`, `tee`, `head`, `xxd`, …). An enumeration of the leaking side has SILENT gaps, so **adding one pipe stage turned a leak the tool already caught into a clean run**: `base64 <secret file>` reddened while `cat <secret file> | base64` did not, and neither did a list of other filters that the tool's own BOUNDS docstring owns (three copies of that enumeration had already diverged by one member each — it is kept in one place now, and this entry points at it). Two other spellings did the same — a pipeline whose head merely READ a secret file marked nothing (the name it is handed is a PATH, so no secret VALUE appeared in any argv), and a trailing `|` at end of line ended the pipeline in the splitter, so the wrapped form of a leak was green while the one-line form reddened. **The predicate is now inverted: a tail leaks unless it is a known stdin SINK** (`STDIN_SINKS` — a digest, a file write, a network send, a program that resolves the value itself). Marking the pipeline from a READER also widens the `log` rule by one real case, pinned as its own leg: `cat "$TOKEN_FILE" >> /var/log/provision.log` was green in **both** directions — captured, so no `stdout` finding, and no secret VALUE in any argv, so no `log` finding either. ⇒ **This is a real change to the bound this entry disclosed.** Everywhere else the tool is still a grep over spellings, and *"it would green on the instrument nobody listed"* still holds; on this one leg it does not — an unlisted tail **reds**, and the doc waives the line with a reason. That direction is the only one a backstop may be wrong in: a false positive is loud and waivable, a false green is neither. **Not flipped to blanket default-deny**, which would have reddened the form the rule PRESCRIBES (`printf … | curl --config -`). ⛔ **The sink list's admission test is now STATED and asserted, because the first draft's claim that it was "derived from the prescribed forms rather than invented" was false of 22 of its 37 members** — `socat`, `msmtp`, `sendmail`, `chpasswd`, `sqlite3`, `psql`, `dd`, `sponge`, `age`, `gpg`/`gpg2`, `ssh`, `nc`, `mysql`, `wc` and the rest appeared in no prescribed form and in no runbook here, and three of them were measurably WRONG: `dd` with no `of=`, `gpg -d` and `ssh host cat` all copy stdin to stdout, so each was a listed sink that leaked in silence. A member is now admitted only by the rule prescribing the instrument (the digest family; a value fed on stdin, worked in the rule as `curl --config -`) or by this repo's runbooks using it (`install`, `php artisan bridge:sign`, the `openssl dgst` it replaced), and a unit test asserts the SET rather than leaving the paragraph to drift from it. The removals buy false positives, which are loud and waivable; keeping them bought silent greens, which are neither. **The cost was measured, not assumed:** re-run over **85 tags / 1,973 tag-file pairs** (`bin/doc-fence-census.py`, 2026-09-01), the inverted predicate — and the trimmed list, and every fix in this entry's review round — reds on **nothing** the enumerating version did not and loses nothing it caught (**399 findings / 5 distinct messages, byte-identical before and after**), and `dev` stays at 0 findings over 29 files. ⚠ **The bound this buys, named:** a sink whose stdout IS a function of its stdin in some other mode is green as a tail — `openssl` is the worked case, listed because `dgst` is a prescribed form, so `| openssl base64` does not red (its argv-borne twin, the DL-322 member, is caught by the `argv` rule and does not depend on this leg). ⚠ **A second false positive is disclosed rather than fixed, and the disclosure itself was wrong the first time:** it is not scoped to an UNQUOTED `<<EOF`. The tool tracks no heredocs at all, so ANY heredoc body — quoted or not — is read as though it were commands, and a secret expansion inside one reports an `argv` finding against what is really a config line. On the quoted `<<'EOF'` form that message is not merely a false positive but a false STATEMENT, since a quoted heredoc expands nothing and no value reaches an argv. Wording, not the parser: teaching it heredocs would be a further change to what CI rejects, and the shape fires on no doc in this repo at any tag. Both forms are pinned by a test so the disclosure cannot go stale, and the waiver is the answer if one appears. *(Sixth round, appended: **this was still the wrong direction.** ANY heredoc body is read as commands, but only a body the reader parses as a COMMAND carrying the secret in an ARGUMENT reds; the config shape a heredoc usually has is SILENTLY GREEN — `token=$SECRET` is eaten whole by the assignment-prefix strip in `_read_command`, `export TOKEN=$SECRET` names a builtin the `argv` rule skips and no printing rule reads, and a bare `$SECRET` line puts the expansion in the command NAME — in every spelling, `<<EOF`, `<<-EOF` and `<<EOF | base64`. So the arm an author SEES is the loud one and the arm that would matter is silent. Both arms are now disclosed and both carry payloads; see the sixth-round bullet below.)* ⚠ **A third bound, found in the same round:** a NESTED command substitution is read one level deep on the secret-FILE leg, so `$(echo "$(cat <secret file>)")` is green where the one-level `$(cat <secret file>)` reds. A nested secret VALUE expansion is unaffected. Recorded, not fixed.

- **⚑ THE SAME REVIEW ROUND FOUND FOUR MORE SILENT GREENS, all of the one shape this entry is about — a spelling detail deciding a security verdict.** Each is now red, each was watched failing first, and the census above is the cost control for all four together. **(1) The continuation test read the CURRENT LINE, not the buffer**, so a blank or comment line after a trailing `|` flushed the pipeline and handed the tail `idx == 0`, where the tail rule cannot run: `echo "$SECRET" |`, a blank line, `base64` was green while the adjacent-line form — fixed earlier in this same entry — reddened. The fix is the same one word: test `buf`, not `code`. **(2) `xargs` sat in `COMMAND_PREFIXES` beside `sudo`**, so it was stripped and `printf … | xargs curl -H` read as ending at `curl`, a known sink. `xargs` converts stdin INTO an argv — it is the DL-322 surface itself, and it is now no more a transparent prefix than `env` is. **(3) The tail rule's `and not secret_files` clause disabled the whole leg for any tail whose argv merely LOOKED like a secret path**, which let `printf '%s' "$SECRET" | diff - <secret file>` through — the *"Compare both values"* member DL-321 fixed, arriving through a pipe. The clause exists to dedupe `tee` (a reader that is also a tail) and is now scoped to exactly that. **(4) The segment splitter treated every `{` and `}` as the shell's group-command syntax**, so `xargs -I{} curl …` reported against a command called `-I` — and, unlooked-for, an unquoted `echo ${SECRET}` was cut into `echo $` + `SECRET` and went GREEN while its quoted twin reddened. Braces now separate only as standalone words. **And one waiver-scope defect:** a pending waiver survived any number of blank lines, so `# doc-fence-lint: allow …` at the top of a fence claimed the first command however far below, against a docstring promising *the line before it*. A blank line drops it now (an intervening comment does not — comments attach to the command they precede, and the docstring says so).

- **⚑ A THIRD ROUND FOUND TWO MORE, AND THE FIRST IS A DUPLICATED PREDICATE RATHER THAN A MISSING ONE.** **(1) *Does this command put a secret FILE on stdout* was answered in two places, and the two disagreed.** `_analyse_pipeline` asked over `args + input_paths()`; `_sub_is_secret_bearing` asked over `args` alone. So the verdict on identical bytes depended on which caller asked: `cat < "$TOKEN_FILE"` reddened on its own line and went GREEN the moment it was captured, and `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat < "$TOKEN_FILE")"` was clean while its `$(cat "$TOKEN_FILE")` twin — the same act, one character apart — reddened. **A redirection character was deciding a security verdict.** One predicate, `_secret_files_on_stdout`, now answers for both callers, and it also covers bash’s `$(<file)`, whose parsed command has an EMPTY name and the path only in the redirect — a third spelling of the one act, never handled at all. That leg is scoped to the substitution caller by construction rather than by a condition: a bare `< file` as a whole command opens the file and prints nothing, and the pipeline reader skips a nameless command before it ever asks. ⇒ **The BOUNDS docstring’s claim that the shell reader “understands … command substitution, redirection” was FALSE for exactly these shapes.** It is made true here rather than weakened, which is the only honest direction for a disclosure that a reader uses to decide what the tool covers. *(Fourth round, appended: **HERE-STRINGS were the third false conjunct of that same sentence** — the reader deleted `<<<…` before tokenizing and handed the piece to the `history` rule alone, so no value rule ever saw it. That conjunct is now true too; see the fourth-round bullet below.)* **(2) `printenv NAME` and `declare -p NAME` COULD NOT FIRE.** Both sit in `PRINTING_COMMANDS`, but the `stdout` arm asks for an argument carrying a `$`-expansion and these take a bare NAME — the value appears nowhere in the source text — so `printenv BRIDGE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` was green while `_is_secret_value_name` already answered True about that very argument. A rule that cannot fire is the shape this whole entry is about, met for the second time inside the fix for it. The bare argument is now tested with `_is_secret_value_name` as well, on the `stdout` leg **only**: `printenv` does fork, but what reaches `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` is the NAME it was asked for, so widening `arg_secrets` instead would have produced an `argv` finding whose message is FALSE. It marks the pipeline for the same reason the reader leg does, and no other — otherwise `printenv <secret> | base64` would be green while `printenv <secret>` reds, which is the one-pipe-stage silencing this entry already fixed once. Both were watched failing before the fix. **Cost re-measured on the same instrument: the census is BYTE-IDENTICAL** — 85 tags / 1,973 tag-file pairs / 399 findings / 5 distinct messages — so the round reds on nothing historical and loses nothing it caught, and this branch scans clean at 0 findings over 29 files (measured here; the `dev` figure above is not re-measured by this round). ⚠ **FOUR BOUNDS ARE NEWLY DISCLOSED AND DELIBERATELY NOT CLOSED**, each measured on this checkout, each a further change to what CI rejects, and none firing on any doc in this repo: a fence inside a **blockquote** (`> ` before the backticks) is not recognised as a fence at all — the opener is matched after leading whitespace only, so the body is invisible rather than unparsed; a **Pandoc / Quarto info string** (braces around the language) is not in `SHELL_INFO`; there is **no fd table**, so `exec 3<` a secret file followed by `cat <&3` is green — the reader’s input path is `&3` and nothing carries the opener’s path forward; and a **`sh -c` / `bash -c` string operand** is not recursed into, exactly as `eval`’s is not, so a single-quoted body is GREEN while a double-quoted one reds under `argv` — correctly, since the PARENT shell expands that one into the child’s argv. **Recursing into `-c` operands and inverting the `READING_COMMANDS` head leg were both proposed in this round and are NOT done here**: each changes what CI rejects and belongs to its own ruling on card#8351.

- **⚑ A FOURTH ROUND FOUND THE WORST OF THEM: AN APOSTROPHE TURNED EVERY VALUE-BEARING RULE OFF, AND A HERE-STRING WAS DELETED BEFORE ANY OF THEM RAN.** **(1) EIGHT hand-rolled copies of one quote-state walk, and the two that decide a VERDICT disagreed with the six that do not.** Six guarded the single-quote toggle with `not in_double`; `_secret_expansions` — which every value-bearing rule is built on — and `_mask_substitutions` tracked `in_single` alone and toggled on any `'`, including one inside `"…"`, where bash holds it literal. So an apostrophe opened a single-quoted region the shell does not have and everything after it went **silently green**. Measured on the very shape DL-321 removed from `docs/multi-host.md`: `echo "Save this token securely: $BRIDGE_CHANNEL_TOKEN"` reddened and `echo "Don’t lose it — save this token: $BRIDGE_CHANNEL_TOKEN"` did not, and the same silent green covered the `argv`, `log`, `probe` and pipeline-tail rules. Through the masker the damage crossed COMMANDS, because that copy runs over the whole logical line: `echo "it's hi" ; curl -H "Bearer $(cat "$TOKEN_FILE")" http://x/` was green while the identical line without the apostrophe reddened. ⇒ **Fixed by DELETING the copies, not by correcting the two** — one `QuoteWalk` now yields `(index, text, in_single, in_double, escaped)` and EVERY quote-walking function in the file reads it, because they differ only in what they DO at each character; a further copy would be free to disagree again, so a test asserts the toggle exists in exactly one place. *(Fifth round, appended: that sentence said "all eight consumers" and the fourth round's own here-string fix made it NINE the same day — a count restating a property the test already guards. The property is named here now and the number is gone.)* **(2) A HERE-STRING carrying a secret VALUE was deleted before any value rule saw it.** `_read_command` cuts `<<<…` out of the text before tokenizing — correct for the `argv` rule, since a here-string is stdin and never reaches `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` — and then handed the cut piece to the `history` rule ALONE. `cat <<<"$BRIDGE_WEBHOOK_SECRET"`, `base64 <<<"$SECRET"`, `tr -d "\n" <<<"$SECRET"` and `cat <<<"$SECRET" >> /var/log/x.log` were all green. It is now asked through `token_carries_secret`, the same predicate an ARGUMENT goes through — not a second parser — and feeds the `stdout` and `log` legs and the pipeline mark; `sha256sum <<<"$(cat "$TOKEN_FILE")"` stays green, because deny-by-default reads the same sink list here as at a pipeline tail. **The `<<<` is now LOCATED on the same walk rather than by a regex over the raw text** — a regex cannot tell a here-string from a quoted string that SPELLS one, which cost nothing while the operand fed only the `history` rule and became a false finding the moment it fed the value rules (`echo 'a <<<"$SECRET"' >> x.log`, measured red on the intermediate build); the operand now also runs to the first UNQUOTED space, and where a command carries several the LAST wins, as the shell does. **(3) A finding whose message named the WRONG DIRECTION.** `printf '%s' "$SECRET" | tee <secret store>` rendered “`tee` puts the contents of `<secret store>` on stdout. Open the file yourself” — `tee` **writes** that path; its stdout is its stdin. The line stays red on the tail message, which is the true one, and the unit test that had pinned the false sentence was CORRECTED rather than preserved. ⚠ **Bounds: `tee <secret store>` OUTSIDE a secret-carrying pipeline still renders the reader message, and it is still the wrong direction there** — closing it means deciding whether that line should red at all (it is the prescribed write form), which is a change to what CI rejects and belongs to its own ruling. **Five disclosed bounds that had no test now have one** — the four measured ones plus the one-level depth limit on a secret-FILE read inside a nested substitution, joining the heredoc case that already had one — each pinning the CURRENT behaviour, so closing a bound reds the suite and forces the disclosure to be rewritten instead of going stale. ⚠ *(Fifth round, appended: as WRITTEN that sentence claimed the set, and the set was not five — **eleven** of the nineteen bounds the docstring disclosed still had no pin. See the fifth-round bullet below; the wording above is narrowed to the five this round actually added, and the completeness claim is now carried by a test rather than by a sentence.)* two were falsified by mutation (adding `{bash}` to `SHELL_INFO`, and recursing `_sub_is_secret_bearing` one level further) and the rest carry the positive payload on the same shape. **Cost, re-measured on the same instrument: the census is BYTE-IDENTICAL again** — 85 tags / 1,973 tag-file pairs / 399 findings / 5 distinct messages, the same five messages at the same first tags — so a round that reddens four new shapes reds on nothing historical and loses nothing it caught; this branch scans clean at **0 findings over 29 files**.

- **⚑ A FIFTH ROUND FOUND THE DISCLOSURE ITSELF: ELEVEN OF NINETEEN BOUNDS HAD NO PIN WHILE THREE SURFACES SAID THE SET WAS CLOSED.** The fourth-round bullet above, `docs/CHANGELOG.md` and the suite's own class docstring each said *"the five disclosed bounds that had no test now have one"*. Five had gained a pin; **eleven had none** — a command PREFIX that takes an operand, bare `env` / `printenv`, `declare -p` / `typeset -p` / `export -p` / `set` with no operand, a `STDIN_SINKS` member whose stdout is its stdin in another mode, `tee` outside a secret-carrying pipeline, a four-space indented block, functions, loops, `eval`, aliases, and a value routed through several variables. The same docstring had said *"the two"* while asserting one a round earlier, which is the tell: **the defect is the COUNT, not the number in it.** ⇒ **Repaired by making the SET checkable rather than by re-counting it.** The module docstring now tags every bound `BOUND(<slug>)`; the suite maps each slug to the test that pins it; and one test asserts the two sets are EQUAL IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, so a bound added to the disclosure with no pin reds, and so does a pin whose tag was deleted. **All twenty bounds are pinned** — the nineteen plus the one this round discloses — each on the CURRENT behaviour with the payload that reds beside it. *(Sixth round, appended: a twenty-FIRST bound is disclosed below, so read this sentence and the "two of the twenty" one after it as the record of THIS round's set rather than as a live count — the live statement is the registry, which is checked, and no LIVE surface carries the number any more — the round-by-round bullets here and in `docs/CHANGELOG.md` still quote the figure that was true when each was written, which is a record of a round and not a claim about today.)* **Where a one-line mutation can CLOSE a bound the pin was watched failing under it** — dropping `timeout` from `COMMAND_PREFIXES`, `openssl` from `STDIN_SINKS`, `tee` from `READING_COMMANDS`, the `(){}` from the splitter's separator set, either half of the tag↔pin registry, and the message's own redaction: 8 mutants, 8 reds, plus a negative control (an unrelated docstring edit) that stays green, so the guard is not simply always-red. **Where no cheap mutation exists** — an indented-block parser, function/loop/alias/`eval` resolution, following a value across an assignment, a whole-environment printer arm — the bound is held instead by the RED TWIN carried in the same test: the payload that must red, beside the payload that must not, which is what makes the green a measurement rather than a fixture. ⚠ **Two of the twenty are FALSE POSITIVES rather than silent greens, and are pinned in that direction on purpose:** `printf … | timeout 5 sha256sum` reds naming a command `5` (a command PREFIX is dropped and its OPERAND is not), and `tee <secret store>` alone renders the READER message, which names the wrong direction because `tee` WRITES that path — the remainder the fourth round disclosed and did not close. Both are loud and waivable, which is why they are disclosed rather than fixed; the pins exist so that fixing either forces the disclosure to move with it. ⚠ **A TWENTIETH BOUND IS NEWLY DISCLOSED AND NOT CLOSED: a pipeline whose TAIL is a group command `{ …; }` or a subshell `( … )` loses the pipeline mark.** `_split_segments` ends the pipeline at the standalone `{` / `(`, so the tail begins a pipeline of its own where `idx > 0` is false and the tail rule never runs: `echo "$SECRET" | { base64; }` and `| (base64)` are GREEN where `| base64` reds, and `|&` is read as `|` followed by a command named `&`, so it reds naming text no doc contains. Carrying the mark across that flush changes what CI rejects and belongs to its own ruling; **measured at 0 occurrences over the 1,973 tag-file pairs** — a deliberately OVER-approximating scan (any `|` before a `{`/`(`, and any `|&`, in any shell fence at any tag) returning zero, against a control showing the same scan sees 499 pipe-carrying lines, so the zero is a measurement and not an empty run — and it is therefore disclosed rather than widened. ⛔ **AND ONE DEFECT IN THE TOOL'S OWN OUTPUT, which is a member of the class this program exists to catch: the `history` finding QUOTED the literal payload into the CI log.** The message rendered *"… is a command-line literal (`<the value>`)"*, republishing the very value the rule keeps off a readable surface into a GitHub Actions log that outlives the branch it was raised on — a force-push takes the head away and leaves the log. It now names the literal by POSITION and LENGTH and never by value (`argument 2, a literal 16 characters long`; `the here-string operand, a literal 11 characters long`), which is still text the author can locate in their own doc and is nothing a log reader can use. **The VERDICT is unchanged** — the same lines red under the same rule on the same surfaces; only the wording moves. **Cost re-measured on the same instrument and the figures are unmoved:** 85 tags / 1,973 tag-file pairs / **399 findings / 5 distinct messages**, the two rewritten `history` messages keeping their counts (84 and 76) and their first tags; this branch scans clean at **0 findings over 29 files**.

- **⚑ A SIXTH ROUND STOPPED PATCHING AND FIXED THE INSTRUMENT: THE FIFTH ROUND'S GUARD COMPARES TWO LISTS OF NAMES, SO A DISCLOSURE COULD BE COMPLETE AND FALSE.** ⛔ **The trend is why this round is shaped differently from the five before it:** rounds three, four, five and six each returned **two** mechanism findings against a subject the previous round had reviewed and called clean. A finding count that stops falling is the pre-committed non-convergence signal, and it says the LOOP is at fault rather than the work — so this round lands the upstream fix the sixth reviewer named instead of a seventh instance patch. **(1) EVERY PIN NOW CARRIES ITS PAYLOAD AND ITS EXPECTED VERDICT AS DATA.** The fifth round's registry proved tag-set == pin-set; - **⛔ WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLOSE.** Not the class. It reads markdown shell fences and nothing else, and only the shapes someone has already seen: a member minted in a `.php`, a `.sh`, a workflow `run:` block, a hook script or prose is out of reach by construction, and so is any spelling the vocabulary does not know. **A green run of this check is not evidence the class is absent** — that sentence is printed by the tool on every clean run precisely so no reader has to come here to find it out.
