## DL-325 — a periodic-job REGISTRY inside the bridge: jobs are data, handlers are the governed surface, and ONE opt-in tick joins the event gate rather than replacing it (card#8425)

- **Date:** 2026-09-01
- **Status:** implemented (card#8425, roundtable #341). ⚠ **ONE MIGRATION** (`scheduled_jobs`) — run `php artisan migrate`. **⚠ THIS ADDS A NEW INGRESS AND NEW PERIODIC EXECUTION.** No receiver accept/reject change, no token-scope change, no change to any existing handler's behaviour. Five new `BRIDGE_JOBS_*` keys, all with safe defaults; **the tick is OPT-IN and an install that changes nothing behaves exactly as it did.**

**Context — an operator-ratified directive, relayed on rt#341, not a proposal.** Its floor was fixed and is not re-litigated here: **one external tick · jobs-as-data · runtime insert/remove, with the crontab line never changing.** The problem it targets is DL-306's own documented dead end, in DL-306's words: *"the pass fires on the first inbound webhook AFTER the interval lapses, so an install receiving nothing pushes nothing."* **An install with no traffic runs NO periodic work at all**, which is precisely the install a watchdog exists to catch — and no arrival-gated mechanism can fix it, because the gate's clock IS the traffic.

- **⚑ Decision 1 — the registry is a TABLE and the API is runtime.** `scheduled_jobs` holds one row per job INSTANCE carrying `{name, handler, interval_s, owner, docs_ref, justification, enabled, payload}` plus the scheduler's own bookkeeping; `App\Bridge\Scheduling\JobRegistry` is `insert` (upsert by name) / `remove` / `setEnabled` / `all`. **A table and not config, and not cache**, for two reasons: the inserter and the runner are different PROCESSES (an FPM worker's after-response callback may insert a job the CLI `bridge:tick` must then see), and the registry is the AUDITABLE BOUNDARY — *"GET the job list and you have named the entire periodic population of this install"* is only true of a durable, single-homed list. An evictable one is a periodic population that silently stops existing, which is DL-012's failure with extra steps.

- **⭐ Decision 2 — HANDLERS ARE THE GOVERNED SURFACE; INSTANCES ARE FREE** (the operator-approved split, adopted verbatim). A row may only name a handler that exists in this build, so what a job *can do* is fixed at code-review time. **An unknown handler is a LOUD REFUSAL, never a silent skip** — refused at insert AND at run, through ONE predicate (`JobHandlerRegistry::refusalFor()`), with the instance recording `refused` + the reason, a `Log::error`, and a `fail` from `bridge:check`. A skip has no vocabulary: a job that quietly does not run is indistinguishable from a job with nothing to do.

- **⭐ Decision 3 — the state-mutating distinction is STRUCTURAL, not a comment.** `JobCapability::{ReadAndAlert, MutatesState}` is declared by the handler, and a `MutatesState` handler is **inert** until this install's operator names it in `BRIDGE_JOBS_ARMED_MUTATORS`. That mechanises *"board/state-mutating handlers require operator approval to exist at all"*: registration is unconditional (so the registry can say *"that handler exists but is not armed"*, a different fact from *"no such handler"*, with a different remedy), and ARMING is the operator act. ⛔ **Bound, stated:** the declaration records what the AUTHOR CLAIMS. A handler that writes to a board while declaring `ReadAndAlert` is mis-declared and nothing here detects it — the mechanism makes the claim reviewable and arming explicit; it does not sandbox.

- **⛔⭐ Decision 4 — THE TICK IS AN ADDITIONAL INGRESS, NEVER A REPLACEMENT, and this amends DL-199.** The registry runs from **either** the after-response event gate (DL-199's shape, on every install, no operator action) **or** `bridge:tick` (one crontab line, opt-in per install). Two reasons, and the second is the one that matters technically:
  1. **An install that has not added the crontab line must keep working exactly as today.** Shipping tick-only would make a crontab line a hard dependency of running the bridge, and every consuming install would have to adopt one operator's mechanism to keep the software working.
  2. **The two ingresses cover DIFFERENT blind spots, so they are not redundant.** The event gate covers the BUSY install and needs no clock; the tick covers the SILENT one, which is the DL-306 gap above. Either alone leaves a real install with no periodic execution.
  ⚠ **DL-199's stated reason for removing the last cron exception is CORRECTED here, not merely narrowed.** That entry attributed the no-cron posture to another install's *"operator-ratified hard constraint"*. Per the operator, that is not what the rule was: it was **ANTI-PROLIFERATION** — it existed to stop multiple agents each reaching for cron as an easy way out — and a **single** crontab line with the bridge owning the job list satisfies it rather than violating it. **The anti-proliferation intent is therefore what this design is built to serve**, and Decision 5 is where it is paid for. DL-199 carries a forward annotation; its own reasoning and all four implementation properties stand.

- **⛔ Decision 5 — EVENT-DRIVEN IS THE DOCUMENTED DEFAULT, and every instance carries a required JUSTIFICATION.** The operator's rule is *"I don't want the default to be to create more cron jobs; I want agents to always consider whether there is a non-cron solution first"* — which is in direct tension with *"instances are free"*, and the tension is resolved WITHOUT gating instance creation:
  - `docs/periodic-jobs.md` **opens** with *a periodic job is the LAST resort*, and its first section is a four-step decision order that points at the event gate, at a consumer pull, and at do-it-when-it-happens **before** it will describe a job at all. The `config/bridge.php` block and the `JobHandler` interface docblock say the same thing, so whatever a future agent reads first pushes it away from cron.
  - **`justification` is a required, non-null column and a required constructor argument on `JobSpec`.** An instance without one is REFUSED at insert. It is returned by the enumeration API and printed under every row by `bridge:jobs`, so the registry audit answers *"why is this periodic?"* rather than only *"what runs?"*.
  - **It is NOT an approval gate.** Nobody is consulted, nothing queues, insertion stays programmatic and runtime, and the answer is never judged. The friction is exactly one sentence, paid by the inserter.
  - ⛔ **Bound, stated plainly, because the mechanism's value depends on it being understood:** a 20-character floor refuses a blank, a dash and an `n/a`; it CANNOT refuse a fluent sentence that is wrong. What it buys is that a reason EXISTS, is attributable, and is read back by every audit — the same thing `App\Bridge\Check\Silence` buys one subsystem over, and for the same reason (a required sentence cannot be added across N call sites without somebody writing N sentences).

- **⚑ Decision 6 — the four DL-199 properties are inherited VERBATIM by the shared pass**, because each is a way to re-create the DL-001 latency regression: **AFTER-RESPONSE** (a terminating callback — job execution is never on a client-visible path), **BOUNDED** (`jobs.max_per_pass`, default 3, oldest-due first), **INTERVAL-GATED** (one `min_pass_interval` marker, **shared by both ingresses**, so a ticked-and-busy install does not double-run), and **NON-BLOCKING `Cache::lock`** — ⛔ **a blocking lock here is FORBIDDEN**: it would queue every concurrent receive behind whatever job is running. Plus **NEVER THROWS PAST THE PASS**, with each job caught INDIVIDUALLY inside the loop so one handler's throw does not cost the others their pass, and `next_due_at` advanced BEFORE the handler runs so a persistently-throwing job retries once per its own interval rather than on every delivery. ⛔ **Swallowing the THROW is not swallowing the FACT, and the exit contract turns on the difference.** `JobPassResult` carries whether the pass RAN and, when it did not, whether that was an ordinary skip (lock lost, inside the shared interval, registry disabled) or a FAULT (the DB unreachable, the cache backend gone, a `BRIDGE_JOBS_*` cadence this install cannot act on). `bridge:tick` and `bridge:jobs run` exit **non-zero on a fault and 0 on every skip** — a crontab line reddening on ordinary skips would mail its operator on most runs of a busy install and the alarm would be filtered within a week. ⚑ The tick's own stamp is written BEFORE the pass either way, so a fault never also reads as a dead clock. ⚠ **The same rule governs the last-pass-failure marker**: only a pass that RAN clears it. Clearing it on any non-throwing return erased the failure on the next skipped pass — seconds later on a busy install — which left `bridge:check`'s error leg dead. ⛔ **AND THE CATCH ARM ITSELF MUST NOT THROW, which it did on the one fault it most needed to survive.** The arm recorded the pass fault by WRITING TO THE CACHE, unguarded, as its first statement — so with the CACHE as the fault it re-raised: no log line, no marker, and the throw escaped the shell. Measured, not reasoned: `bridge:tick` died at `TickRecord::stamp()` with a stack trace (exit 1 *by accident*, and no summary line), and `JobSchedulerGate`'s terminating callback ended every delivery with an unhandled fatal in the FPM worker, because `Application::terminate()` has no try/catch. The three sentences above were false for that fault until fault recording moved into **`App\Bridge\Support\FaultMarker`** — one primitive that **logs first and writes the marker second, each leg guarded** — and `TickRecord` learned to treat a stamp it cannot write as `unmeasured` rather than as a throw. ⚠ On a dead cache the LOG is the only surviving record; the marker lives in the store that failed. ⛔ **And if BOTH legs are down — one cause does it, since the default config writes the log to `storage/logs` and the `file` cache to `storage/framework/cache/data` — what happens next differs BY CALLER, so it is stated per caller rather than promised for all three.** On the TICK path the fact still rides the RESULT: `JobScheduler::passSafely()` returns a `JobPassResult`, and `bridge:tick` / `bridge:jobs run` read `passFailed()` off it and exit non-zero. On the OTHER paths it does not: `RetentionGate::runSafely()` and `StandupGate::runSafely()` are `void` terminating callbacks with no result to carry, and `JobSchedulerGate` — the event ingress — calls the same `passSafely()` from a terminating callback that DISCARDS its return value. A simultaneous log-and-cache failure on those three is UNREPORTED, and that is accepted here: the alternative is re-raising out of a terminating callback, which is the defect this whole strand exists to end. ⚑ Every existing test of "never throws past the pass" broke the DATABASE, which leaves the recorder working — the fault has to be injected into the RECORDER for the promise to be falsifiable (`Tests\Fixtures\DeadBackend`).

- **⭐ Decision 7 — DEATH IS THE ALARM, and only a DECLARATION can arm it.** The tick is the single point of failure on an install that adopted it, and its failure mode is silence — `bridge:prune` sat unscheduled ~45 days across three installs (DL-012) for exactly that reason. `bridge:tick` stamps a last-tick record **before** it works (the record answers *"is the clock alive?"*, so it must be written by the clock firing, not by the pass going well), and freshness is judged against **`BRIDGE_JOBS_TICK_EXPECTED_EVERY` — this install's own declaration, never a fleet-wide constant**, because only this install knows what its crontab line says. `bridge:jobs --assert-tick` exits non-zero for a session-start hook; `bridge:check`'s `jobs.posture` leg discloses the same fact at preflight. **⚑ The event gate deliberately does NOT stamp the record**: a busy install stamping it from traffic would answer *"is anything arriving?"* in a field that reads as *"is the clock alive?"* — the exact class DL-306 refused for the digest.

- **⭐ Decision 8 — FOUR tick states, because a three-way alarm pages the wrong installs.** Derived from the ruling on staleness rather than from convenience: `unmeasured` (**an absent record is UNMEASURED, not stale — never read absence as death**, and this is also the ordinary state of every un-adopted install), `undeclared` (a record with no declared horizon: an age is known, **no verdict is claimed**, because inventing a default constant to produce one is exactly what a per-record threshold refuses), `fresh`, and `stale`. **Only a declared horizon can fail an assertion**, so this cannot be adopted by accident. ⚠ A cache flush loses the stamp and degrades to `unmeasured` — loud on a declared install, silent on an undeclared one, and **never a false `fresh`**.

- **⚠ Decision 9 — the staleness ruling for OTHER records is recorded as a binding contract and NOT implemented, because the bridge has no record to implement it against.** The rt#341 ruling — *the threshold lives on the RECORD, not on the watchdog; a writer declares its own expected-next-boundary; no horizon ⇒ a weaker verdict (`suspect`, never `wedged`) and a NUDGE, never anything destructive; an ABSENT record is UNMEASURED; `interval_s` survives only on records the scheduler itself emits* — is written into `docs/periodic-jobs.md` § *Staleness of things that are NOT the tick* as binding on any watchdog handler added here. **Building the evaluator now would be building for a state that cannot happen** (canon #6): no seat-state record exists in this repository, so a `suspect` branch would be unreachable code shipped against a schema this build cannot read. What IS implemented is the same rule applied to the one record this change ships — the tick's own freshness (Decision 8).

- **⚑ Decision 10 — ONE shipped handler, and it is `standup_digest` rather than a demo.** It delegates to `StandupGate::runPass()` (made public for it) instead of re-implementing the pass, so **both ingresses share the digest's own interval marker and one digest is pushed however many things asked** — a second implementation would push a second digest at somebody's live session. It is `ReadAndAlert` (it reads and pushes; it mutates no board state), so it needs no arming. Chosen because DL-306 is the one shipped subsystem with a documented dead end only a clock can close, which makes it the honest first instance. ⚑ Two intervals with different meanings, documented: the INSTANCE's `interval_s` is how often the scheduler **asks**; `standup.interval` is how often the digest is **pushed**.

- **Alternatives considered:**
  - **Tick-only (delete the event-gated path).** Rejected — Decision 4. It makes a crontab line a hard dependency of running the bridge for every consuming install, and it loses nothing to keep both, because the two cover different blind spots.
  - **An HTTP tick endpoint instead of an artisan command.** Rejected: it adds a second authenticated ingress to a receiver whose whole surface is one HMAC-verified route, and it would put job execution behind a request — the one thing this design must not do. A crontab line calling `php artisan bridge:tick` is the same "one line" with no new door.
  - **A `justification` that is optional, or a lint that reads it.** The first discharges the operator's rule with a field nobody fills; the second judges prose, which is unfalsifiable. A required argument with a floor that refuses only a non-answer is the honest middle, and its bound is stated in Decision 5 rather than implied.
  - **Approval-gating instance creation for state-mutating handlers.** Rejected: it contradicts the directive's floor (runtime insert/remove is ungated) AND is redundant — the handler is already inert unless armed, so the gate would be paid twice for one guarantee.
  - **Keeping the last-tick record in the DATABASE.** Rejected: a write per tick plus a schema for one timestamp, to buy survival across a cache flush — and the flush's failure direction is already safe (`unmeasured`, never `fresh`). It also uses the same store the DL-199 gates already depend on, so it adds no infrastructure.
  - **Registering the check under the existing `CheckSlot::Retention` to avoid touching `handle()`.** Rejected: it would make that slot's docblock false and hide a second subject inside a named position, to dodge a doc banner the repository already has a mechanism for.
  - **Hoisting `JobHandlerRegistry` onto `App\Bridge\Support\HandlerRegistry`.** ⚑ **Not done here, and it is a second duplication to watch beside the gate one below.** The two classes carry the same register/resolve/known shape over different handler contracts, and `JobHandlerRegistry` adds the arming predicate the dispatch registry has no analogue for. Collapsing them would need a generic keyed-registry primitive both specialise, which is a refactor of a shipped, on-every-delivery class on a PR that already adds an ingress. Recorded rather than left to be rediscovered at the third registry.
  - **Migrating `RetentionGate` and `StandupGate` onto the new scheduler as job instances.** ⚑ **Not done here, and it is the shape to watch.** Those two plus `JobSchedulerGate` are now THREE users of the after-response gate shape; the interval marker, the non-blocking lock, the never-throws shell and the error-key are re-stated in each. This change deliberately did NOT re-home the other two — that changes the behaviour of two shipped, on-by-default subsystems on a PR that already adds a new ingress — but it is a real duplication and the next gate written must consolidate rather than add a fourth. Filed as **card#8432**, which carries the consolidation's fix shape and the block it puts on the next gate (canon #18: an open class item blocks its symptoms) — a follow-up with a number, not a note left to be rediscovered. ⛔ **ONE STRAND OF IT IS CONSOLIDATED HERE, BECAUSE IT WAS NOT A STYLE PROBLEM BUT A LIVE DEFECT IN ALL THREE COPIES**: each arm's *"record the fault"* wrote to the cache unguarded and re-raised when the cache was the fault, so all three shells could throw out of a terminating callback. They now share `App\Bridge\Support\FaultMarker` (log first, marker second, each leg guarded, one TTL floor). ⚠ **That is the ARM only** — the interval marker, the non-blocking lock and the pass shell are still restated in each gate, and re-homing retention and standup as job instances remains the follow-up above.

- **⚠ WHAT CHANGES FOR AN EXISTING INSTALL.** **Nothing, unless the operator acts.** `jobs.enabled` defaults TRUE, but the registry is EMPTY by default, so the whole cost is one indexed `scheduled_jobs` query at most once per `min_pass_interval` on delivery, and `bridge:check`'s new `jobs.posture` leg yields NOTHING on an install with no rows and no declared tick — measured, not argued: every one of the committed golden captures changed by **one line per file and no finding content** — the inventory line, whose counts moved by one. Adopting the tick is one crontab line plus one `.env` key, both documented in `docs/periodic-jobs.md`. **`php artisan migrate` IS required** — without it, the `jobs.posture` leg reports `unvalidated` naming the unmigrated install, and a pass records itself as failed in the last-pass-error marker rather than failing a webhook.

- **Consequences:** new `app/Bridge/Scheduling/` (`JobCapability`, `JobHandler`, `JobContext`, `JobOutcome`, `JobRefusal`, `JobHandlerRegistry`, `JobSpec`, `JobSpecException`, `JobRegistry`, `JobScheduler`, `JobPassSource`, `JobPassResult`, `JobSchedulerGate`, `TickRecord`, `TickState`, `TickPosture`, `Handlers/StandupDigestJob`); new `App\Models\ScheduledJob` + its migration; new `bridge:tick` and `bridge:jobs`; new `App\Bridge\Check\Checks\JobsPostureCheck` in a new `CheckSlot::Jobs`. `WebhookController` schedules the third gate; `StandupGate::runPass()` is public and its docblock records why. New `App\Bridge\Support\FaultMarker`, and `RetentionGate`/`StandupGate`/`JobScheduler` all record through it (see Decision 6); `Tests\Fixtures\DeadBackend` makes the recorder itself the fault. Five new `BRIDGE_JOBS_*` keys (`config/bridge.php`, `.env.example`, `docs/config-schema.md`, `CLAUDE_DEPLOYMENT.md`), resolved and validated once in `App\Bridge\Scheduling\JobsConfig` — the `RetentionConfig` shape, and for its reason: the scheduler acts on the posture and `bridge:check` reports it, so a second derivation is a preflight describing a cadence the receiver is not running. ⛔ **A cadence value outside its bound is REFUSED, never clamped**: `max(1, (int) …)` turned `BRIDGE_JOBS_MIN_PASS_INTERVAL=sixty` into a ONE-SECOND floor — a registry pass on every delivery — silently. It now runs no pass and the `jobs.posture` leg fails naming the key. New `docs/periodic-jobs.md`. **Every committed golden capture was regenerated for the inventory total only** — how many there are is the harness's to state (`CLAUDE_TESTING.md` § *The `bridge:check` golden harness*), never this entry's, so no capture count is restated here — and `docs/check-golden-coverage.md` carries BOTH the STALE and SUBJECT MOVED banners: `handle()` gained one predicate (the `CheckSlot::Jobs` emit), and the ~50-minute mutation run was deliberately not re-run for it — the banners are the repository's own sanctioned disclosure for exactly this, and its verdict tables were already documented as unguarded. ⚑ **DL-306 declined a `bridge:check` posture leg "on cost rather than principle" — that cost is paid here**, once, for a leg whose silence on an unadopted install is itself pinned.

- **Bounds, stated.** **NOT EXERCISED ON A LIVE CRONTAB.** `bridge:tick` is exercised by the suite as an artisan invocation with no webhook ever delivered — which is the property that matters (periodic work at zero traffic) — but no crontab line has been installed and watched fire on a host. The freshness horizon's jitter grace (one extra interval + 60s) is a judgement, not a measurement. **THE `justification` FLOOR CANNOT JUDGE A REASON** (Decision 5). **THE CAPABILITY DECLARATION IS A CLAIM, NOT A SANDBOX** (Decision 3). **ONE SHIPPED HANDLER**, so the handler contract has exactly one production implementation plus the suite's; a second one may find the `JobContext`/`JobOutcome` shape wanting. **THE THREE-GATE DUPLICATION IS OPEN**, disclosed in the alternatives above rather than absorbed silently.

## DL-329 — the CHANGELOG gate discriminates the PRE-FOLD cause and tells the author to MOVE the entry, not to add a second one; the verdict is untouched (card#8339)

**Status:** implemented (card#8339). Diagnostic only — **what CI accepts and rejects is byte-for-byte unchanged**; every arm that exited 1 still exits 1, and every arm that exited 0 still exits 0. No migration, no config key, no `.env` change, no token-scope change, no receiver accept/reject change.

**Context.** The release fold (VERSIONING.md § Release flow step 4) renames `## [Unreleased]` to `## [X.Y.Z]` and opens a fresh empty one above it. That is an **insertion**: the entries are not moved, the heading above them is. A branch cut before the fold therefore carries its entry under text git now reads as `[X.Y.Z]`, its own side of that text is unchanged, and the 3-way merge has no reason to relocate it — so the branch merges **cleanly** and files its entry inside a **released** section, which then claims work that release did not ship, while the real `[Unreleased]` is empty and the change is invisible to the next release. Verified on the card with `git merge-tree --write-tree`; it recurs for **every in-flight branch at every release**, and two instances landed in one cycle.

`changelog-gate.yml` was already RED on it — both arms of its own logic fail here — so this was never a correctness escape. The defect was that its message named the wrong cause: *"Fix: add an `[Unreleased]` entry citing `card#NNNN`"*. An author who follows that literally files a **second** entry and leaves the first corrupting the released section. Measured on run 33544122079: card#8351's entry was standing under `[0.80.0]` while the gate told the author to add one.

- **⚑ Decision 1 — fix the DIAGNOSTIC, not the verdict.** The detection runs only after the gate has already decided to fail, and it chooses which remedy is printed. A gate whose accept-set moves is an ask-first change (CLAUDE.md always-ask); a gate that reaches the same verdict and explains it correctly is not, and it is also the fix with the higher value — the recurrence is paid by an author who now knows what to do in one read instead of minting a duplicate entry.
- **⚑ Decision 2 — read the MERGED tree, and read the SAME one the verdict came from.** On a `pull_request` event `actions/checkout` checks out `refs/pull/<n>/merge` (measured in run 33544122079: `git checkout --force refs/remotes/pull/628/merge`), so `docs/CHANGELOG.md` in the working tree already IS the merge — which is the only reason the gate could see the defect at all, since on the branch alone the entry sits under a heading still spelled `[Unreleased]`. The diagnosis is carved from that same file rather than from a fresh `git merge-tree`: a second reading of "the merged changelog" could contradict the verdict it exists to explain.
- **⚑ Decision 3 — a MODE on `bin/changelog-section.py`, not a second script.** `--locate-added` reuses the one section-boundary carve (`_sections`, which `extract` now also calls) to answer *which released section carries a line this branch introduced*. A sibling script would be DL-276's own rationale inverted — two carvings that disagree about where a section ends is the defect class the single extractor exists to prevent.
- **⚑ Decision 4 — the needles are the branch's own NEW lines, and the baseline subtraction is load-bearing.** Candidates come from `git diff $BASE...$HEAD -- docs/CHANGELOG.md` (merge-base, so the base's own changes are not attributed to this branch), minus every line the base changelog already carried. Without the subtraction a branch adding a `### Fixed` head under `[Unreleased]` would match the identical head in a released section and be told it had made a mistake it did not make. The residual is the safe direction: a branch line that duplicates an existing one is dropped, which loses the diagnosis rather than inventing one.
- **⚑ Decision 5 — the label is not the diagnosis: the fold is ASSERTED, not inferred — and asserted from the branch's FORK POINT.** ⚠ **These two legs are not the whole predicate — Decision 7 RE-DERIVES it, and Decision 8 corrects the SPELLING of the fork-point read; this decision is read through both.** **The fold remedy fires only when the released section carrying the branch's line DOES exist on `$BASE` and did NOT exist at the branch's fork point — the parent of the oldest commit on the branch's own first-parent line (`git rev-list --topo-order --first-parent $HEAD ^$BASE | tail -1`) — i.e. that section was cut while this branch was open.** The label alone establishes something weaker: *a line this branch adds sits in a released section of the merged tree*, which two other shapes satisfy while the sentence *"v X.Y.Z was cut while this branch was open"* is FALSE of both. Each is now a fixture, and each was watched printing the wrong remedy before the predicate went in. (a) **The branch CORRECTS a line inside a section that already stood at its fork point** — the canon-#16 stale-fix shape: the message dated the fold to a window it did not happen in and told the author to lift a **shipped** line out of a release. (b) **The branch CUTS the section itself** — a PR that adds `## [X.Y.Z]` and files under it was told X.Y.Z "was cut while this branch was open" by somebody else. Both new reads go through **the same `bin/changelog-section.py`** the label came from, never a `grep '## [X.Y.Z]'`: a second carve of the section boundary is DL-276's defect class one level down, and it is the reason this predicate is not spelled inline. The verdict is untouched by the extra reads — they run inside `prefold_heading`, whose every non-zero rc still collapses through Decision 6. **⚠ THE FIRST SPELLING OF THIS PREDICATE READ `git merge-base`, AND IT WAS FALSE ON THE ONE SHAPE THIS REMEDY ITSELF CREATES** (found in review, before merge). The remedy's own first step is *merge the base branch*; a branch that takes it makes `$BASE` its own merge-base, so the fold heading stands in the merge-base tree, the predicate goes false, and the gate answers the author — at the exact moment they did what it asked — with the generic *add an `[Unreleased]` entry*, which `docs/CHANGELOG.md` itself names as the opposite of the right move. **A merge is not a re-fork:** *was the fold cut while this branch was open* is a question about where the branch STARTED, and the fork point is the one reading of the history a merge does not move. The needle diff keeps its **merge-base** anchor deliberately, and that is not an inconsistency — it asks what the branch ADDS to the base's text, which a merge of the base does not change, while the predicate asks where the branch began, which a merge does. **The remedy also keeps its `merge the base branch, then MOVE …` step**: it is not redundant — on the un-merged branch the entry still sits under a heading spelled `[Unreleased]`, so there is nothing to relocate yet — and it is no longer a trap, because the state that instruction creates is exactly the state the fork-point predicate still diagnoses.
- **⛔ Decision 6 — an unestablished diagnosis prints the ORIGINAL message.** Every non-zero rc from the locate — no released section carries a branch line, an unreadable input, an empty baseline — collapses to "not established", and the arm falls back to the text it always printed. **The collapse belongs at the TOP of `prefold_heading` and nowhere inside it**, because one of the two section reads is INVERTED: `! changelog_has_section` maps a tooling failure to success — to *the fold heading was absent here* — which is a confident wrong diagnosis carved out of an error. The helper therefore answers three states (0 present · 1 absent, the extractor's own rc 3 · 2 could-not-tell) and the fork-point leg accepts only 1. `bin/changelog-section.py` was leaving a non-UTF-8 file on the interpreter's uncaught-exception exit 1 — `UnicodeDecodeError` is not an `OSError` — and now exits on the usage code like every other unreadable input, so state 2 is reachable by its own rc rather than by luck. Both halves are pinned: a fixture breaks the fork-point read alone (the base and the merged tree stay readable), and re-collapsing that leg to `!` reds it. An empty baseline is refused explicitly rather than read as *a base with no lines*, because that reading inverts the safe direction: with no baseline every added line becomes a needle and a failed `git show` upstream becomes a **confident wrong** diagnosis instead of silence. **⚠ THIS SENTENCE READ "THREE RESIDUALS, ALL IN THE SAME DIRECTION" AND THAT WAS FALSE — corrected 2026-09-01 (review round 3).** There was a FOURTH, running the OTHER way: a branch that forked pre-fold, merged the folded base and then corrected a line the fold had already shipped got the fold remedy asserted at it, on a SHIPPED line. Decision 7 closes that one; the three below remain, and they are the ones that are in the safe direction. **THREE RESIDUALS, in the same direction — the message the gate always printed, never an asserted fold.** (1) **A branch line that DUPLICATES one the base already carried** is subtracted with the `### Fixed` heads (Decision 4), so there is no label to diagnose from. (2) **The non-fold shapes above** produce a label and fail the predicate, so the author gets the message the gate always printed — which is the correct instruction for each: shape (a) needs an `[Unreleased]` entry beside the correction, shape (b) needs one beside the section it cut, and the post-merge correction of Decision 7 needs one beside its correction. (3) **A branch with NO commit of its own, or whose own FIRST commit — the oldest on the branch's OWN first-parent line — is a MERGE or a root commit.** There is then no fork point to read at all, or the commit whose parent would name it has more than one parent, and choosing among them would be a second inference — the thing this predicate exists to remove — so `branch_fork_point` refuses rather than picks, and a genuinely pre-fold branch of that shape goes undiagnosed. **⚠ THIS RESIDUAL WAS FALSE ON BOTH HALVES AS IT STOOD, and Decision 8 is the correction (2026-09-02, review round 4).** It read: *"a branch … whose own oldest commit is a MERGE (or a root commit) … all of a merge's parents are on the base side, so 'the' fork point is a choice between them … so the predicate refuses rather than picks."* Neither half held. **Not all of them are on the base side:** a branch whose own first commit merges a still-unmerged SIBLING has that merge's second parent INSIDE `$HEAD ^$BASE`. **And it did not refuse:** the function never read the branch's own first commit at all — it took the oldest commit of the RANGE, which in that shape is the SIBLING's first commit, single-parent, which the ≠1-parent test ACCEPTS. It therefore returned the SIBLING's fork point, and where the sibling was cut pre-fold the gate asserted *"the branch predates the fold"* at a branch that forked AFTER it. Measured in a constructed cell and control-verified against the `git merge-base` spelling, which refuses that cell correctly. **What prints is the generic `add an [Unreleased] entry`, and on a genuinely pre-fold branch that is NOT "a message that is still correct"** — it is the wrong instruction, the very one this diagnostic exists to stop giving. The trade is taken anyway, and stated rather than claimed harmless: the other direction asserts a fold nobody established and sends the author to edit a RELEASED section. Unhelpful beats confidently wrong. **⚠ THE BOUND THAT STOOD HERE WAS MEASURED OVER THE WRONG POPULATION, and Decision 8 closes the mechanism it was bounding (2026-09-02, review round 4).** It bounded the fork-point risk by counting ranges with MORE THAN ONE ROOT: of the 206 merges reachable from the integration branch — 107 of them PR merges on its first-parent chain — exactly one range carried two roots (PR #399, `sync/main-to-dev-post-v0.70.0`), exempt by head ref before the step reaches any of this and refused again by `branch_fork_point`. ⛔ **That census is not wrong; it is about something else.** The misclassification in residual (3) above fires on a range with exactly ONE root, so root COUNT was never the denominator. **The population that matters is PR ranges where the two readings `branch_fork_point` could take DISAGREE** — the oldest commit of the RANGE versus the oldest commit on the branch's own first-parent line. **Re-derived over every PR range on the integration branch** (each 2-parent merge on its first-parent chain, `BASE=M^1`, `HEAD=M^2`, exactly as the gate is handed them; 536 first-parent commits, 428 with one parent, 107 with two, none with more): **107 ranges · 57 where the two readings disagree · 57 of the 57 on `sync/*` head refs, which this step EXEMPTS · 0 non-exempt.** Two further measurements over the same 57, because the earlier bound leaned on the wrong one: **56 of the 57 were SILENTLY ACCEPTED** by the pre-Decision-8 spelling — the range's oldest commit had exactly one parent, so it returned a fork point taken off another branch's line — and only ONE was refused by it (PR #91, `sync/main-to-dev-post-v0.26.0`, whose range-oldest commit is itself a merge). ⛔ **PR #399, the range the old bound rested on, is not even in this set:** both readings return the same commit there and both refuse it, which is the sense in which the old census answered a different question. **All 57 are refused** by the first-parent spelling, so no diagnosis changes on any of them. The conclusion the earlier bound reached — no reachable non-exempt instance — SURVIVES; its stated evidence did not. The derivation is a script over the live history rather than a recorded figure, and its null control (the same walk compared with itself over the same 107 ranges) reports 0 disagreements. **What is no longer disclosed at all is the ORDERING:** `--topo-order` alone left which root comes last to something git does not document, and a first-parent walk is a single chain with no root to choose among (Decision 8). **A tooling failure inside the diagnosis now says so** — `::notice::changelog pre-fold diagnosis unavailable: <reason>`, on stderr, which the runner still reads workflow commands off — because `heading=$(prefold_heading) || heading=''` is otherwise silent about the difference between *not this shape* and *the read broke*.
- **⚑ Decision 7 — THE PREDICATE IS RE-DERIVED, not patched: it has THREE legs, because legs 1–2 answer a question about the HISTORY while the remedy makes a claim about a LINE.** (Review round 3, 2026-09-01.) **The loop's own non-convergence signal fired first and is why this is a re-derivation rather than a third shape patch:** round 2's must-fix and round 3's are the SAME class — *a state created by the remedy's own first instruction ("merge the base branch"), which the fork-point predicate then misclassifies*. Round 2's instance was the merge making `$BASE` its own merge-base; round 3's is the shape below. Two corrections of one class means the predicate was derived from the wrong question, not spelled wrongly.
  - **The shape (K).** A branch forks pre-fold, **merges the folded base** — exactly what the remedy's first line tells the author to do — and then EDITS a line inside the just-folded `[X.Y.Z]` section. Every input the predicate had holds: the section stands on `$BASE`, it was ABSENT at the fork point, and the corrected line is a line this branch adds sitting under a released heading. So the gate asserted the fold and told that author to **MOVE a SHIPPED line out of a release** — shape (a)'s harm, arriving by a route the fork-point leg cannot see.
  - **Why no reading of the history closes it.** The three trees the predicate can read — fork point, base, merged — are **byte-identical** whether the fold CARRIED that line in or the author WROTE it there after merging. The difference is not in any tree; it is in the branch's own `-` side. A tighter spelling of legs 1–2 is therefore impossible in principle, which is what makes this a third QUESTION.
  - **Leg 3 — the branch deletes no line of that section as the section stands on `$BASE`.** A fold carries lines in and deletes none; a correction DELETES the line it replaces. The `-` side comes off the **same one `$BASE...$HEAD` diff** the needles come off (a second `git diff` could answer a question the first did not), and it is compared with `grep -qxF -f` against the section body produced by **the same extractor read leg 1 already makes** — so "restricted to that section" is the comparison itself and no section boundary is re-derived (DL-276 again). Same three-state rc discipline as leg 2: only grep's own rc 1 means *deletes none*; rc 2 is *could not tell* and drops the diagnosis. **Two filters on that side are load-bearing rather than tidy, and each is pinned by its own fixture:** blank deletions are dropped, because `grep -x -f` reads an empty pattern line as matching every blank line and every section body has them, so one deleted blank anywhere in the changelog would otherwise throw the diagnosis away; and the side is read under **`--output-indicator-old='<'`**, because under the default indicator a deleted line whose own text starts with `-- ` prints as `--- text`, indistinguishable from the `--- a/path` header the awk must skip — a MISSED deletion, which is the unsafe direction (it KEEPS a diagnosis leg 3 would have dropped). The `+` side keeps the default indicator deliberately: a missed needle there only loses the diagnosis.

A and G (true pre-fold, and pre-fold-then-merged) stay green: they delete nothing. Dropping the leg reds 3; inverting it reds 7, in both directions at once.
- **⚑ Decision 8 — the fork-point read walks the branch's OWN first-parent line, not everything the range contains.** (Review round 4, 2026-09-02.) `git rev-list --topo-order $HEAD ^$BASE | tail -1` is the oldest commit IN THE RANGE, and that is the branch's own first commit only when the range holds nothing but this branch's line. **The cell that falsifies it:** a branch forked AFTER the fold whose own FIRST commit merges a sibling cut BEFORE it and not yet on the base. The sibling's commits are then inside the range, its first commit is the range's oldest, it has exactly one parent — so the ≠1-parent refusal never fires — and `branch_fork_point` hands back the SIBLING's fork point, a PRE-fold tree, for a branch that forked after the fold. Legs 1 and 3 hold on that cell, so the gate printed *"the branch predates the fold"* at a branch that does not, and told its author to move a line out of a release. **The range has exactly ONE root, which is why the multi-root bound above never covered it.** **The fix is the WALK, not a further test: `--first-parent`.** The question *where was this branch cut from* is a question about the branch's own line of development, and a first-parent walk is that line; its oldest commit not reachable from `$BASE` is the branch's own first commit by construction, and its first parent is on the base side. `--topo-order` is kept for the ordering guarantee (no parent before its child, so `tail -1` is the oldest), and the ≠1-parent refusal is kept for the shape it was always about — a branch whose own first commit IS a merge, which now includes the cell above. **⛔ The post-hoc check the review recommended does NOT discriminate, and that is measured rather than argued:** *refuse when the RESULT is not on `$HEAD`'s first-parent chain* passes in the cell, because the fork point returned is a base-side commit in BOTH readings and therefore lies on that chain either way. What differs is the commit the fork point is taken FROM, which is what fixing the walk selects. **Blast radius: still diagnostic only.** The change can only make `branch_fork_point` REFUSE where it used to answer, and a refusal collapses through Decision 6 to the message the gate always printed; no arm's exit code moves. Measured over the population in Decision 6: of the 57 PR ranges where the two readings disagree, all 57 are `sync/*`, which the step exempts before it reaches this code — so no PR that has ever run through this gate would have been diagnosed differently. **Controls.** The cell is a fixture (`test_a_post_fold_branch_whose_first_commit_merges_a_pre_fold_sibling_is_not_told_a_fold_happened`) built as a real repo — sibling cut pre-fold, fold on the base, PR branch cut post-fold whose first commit merges the sibling — and it asserts its own discriminating property (the range's oldest commit IS the sibling's, and it has exactly one parent) so it cannot pass for a reason unrelated to the leg. Removing `--first-parent` reds it and nothing else: **RED ×1**. Re-measured at this head, spellings named: dropping the fork-point leg **RED ×3** (×2 before this fixture — the third is it); inverting the leg `-eq 0` **RED ×5** and `-ne 1` **RED ×6**, both unchanged, because the refusal aborts the chain before the leg is reached; reading `git merge-base` instead **RED ×1**, unchanged, and GREEN on this cell — merge-base refuses it correctly, which is how the cell was found. **Residual, in the safe direction:** a genuinely pre-fold branch whose own first commit is a merge (of a sibling, or of the base) now loses its diagnosis instead of getting one off another branch's fork point. That is residual (3) above, and it is the trade this predicate takes everywhere.
- **Alternatives considered.**
  - **Have the fold insert the version heading so pre-fold entries anchor above it, or carry a permanent sentinel under `[Unreleased]`** (the card's structural option). Not adopted: it changes the release act itself for every future release to fix a message, and the anchoring it needs is a property of git's 3-way merge rather than of the file — it would have to be re-verified against every merge strategy, where this reads the merged result directly.
  - **`merge=union` on `docs/CHANGELOG.md`.** Not re-argued: the toolkit measured it and dropped it — GitHub's server-side merge does not apply a `.gitattributes` merge driver (409 where local `git merge-tree` was clean).
  - **Document the relocation step and stop there.** Done as well (VERSIONING.md step 4 now names it), not instead: a runbook line is read at release time by the person cutting the release, and the person who needs it is the author of an in-flight branch reading a CI failure.

Extractor, against `bin/test_changelog_section.py`: drop the baseline subtraction, stop skipping `[Unreleased]`, match the section header line too, accept an empty baseline, delete the blank-needle filter, and leave `UnicodeDecodeError` uncaught — **RED ×1 each**, six for six. ⚠ *The last of those reds the PYTHON suite only: an uncaught traceback exits 1, and `changelog_has_section` classifies rc 1 exactly as it classifies rc 2 — could-not-tell — so the workflow suite stays green under it, and the row says which suite discriminates.* Workflow arms: the pre-fold arm never fires — **RED ×5**; the arm fires on the label alone (the pre-round-1 predicate) — **RED ×7**. ## DL-326 — a seat may CORRECT a card it filed: `board_correct_card` scopes on the mint stamp `board_create_card` already writes, and never widens past what create would accept (card#8378)

**Status:** implemented (card#8378, rt#393 origin). ⚠ **ADDS A WRITE SURFACE — it changes what the bridge accepts on the board-tools door** (operator-gated on the card before implementation). No migration, no new config key, no `.env` change, and nothing the RECEIVER accepts or rejects moves. ⚠ **NEW AUTHORIZATION REQUIREMENT ON THE WRITEBACK USER'S BOARD ROLE — this is the FIRST board tool whose write needs `task.update`.** kanban authorizes a card PATCH by which fields it carries: `TaskMutator::update()` authorizes `move` only when the PATCH's SOLE key is `workflow_stage_id` and `update` for every other field set (kanban DL-204) → `TaskPolicy::update` → `BoardPermissions::TASK_UPDATE`, one of the four slots (`create`/`update`/`move`/`delete`) a `board_custom` role grants INDEPENDENTLY from its pivot JSON (`CUSTOM_TASK_SLOT_MAP`). `board_correct_card` PATCHes `name`/`description`/`tags` and is never stage-only, so **every** call takes `task.update` — where the two existing board tools need only `board.view` (`board_my_cards`) and `task.create` (`board_create_card`). A writeback user on a kanban **Member** role already holds it and is unaffected; one on a custom role narrowed to moves + creates gets a **permanent 403 on every correction**, reported as the install-fault refusal below and never a silent skip. The Sanctum token ABILITY set is unchanged (`write`, which every bridge PATCH already needs). Declared in `docs/kanban-integration-contract.md` §2 and `docs/writeback.md` § *A least-privilege writeback token*. Extends DL-217's tool contract; the channel-server snapshot goes **0.9.8 → 0.9.9** (DL-038).

**Context.** An impl seat's entire board surface was **create + read** — `BoardToolsRegistry` registered `BoardMyCardsTool` and `BoardCreateCardTool` and nothing else, and `board_patch`/`board_update` returned zero hits across `app`, `docs` and `config`. So the only available response to a card the seat itself filed wrongly was to mint a SECOND card, which then defeats every downstream instrument that keys on one card per subject and makes "two problems" indistinguishable from "one problem filed twice" in any audit. ⛔ **`kbcard patch` is not the answer and is not offered as one**: it carries exactly the corrective setters, and it is a local CLI needing a board API token an impl seat does not hold. This was not "exists but scoped wrong" — there was no impl-reachable patch surface at all.

- **⚑ Decision 1 — the scoping rule is *you may correct what you minted*, and the discriminator ALREADY EXISTED.** `BoardCreateCardTool` stamps `created-by:<agent>` on every card it creates, and that tag is caller-unforgeable: `created-by:` is in the reserved prefix set and the guard casefolds, so no caller can plant any case variant of another agent's stamp. Nothing had to be minted for provenance — the first question the card asked. ⛔ **NOT `actor_type`, and NOT `actor_id`.** `actor_type: service` covers the bridge and every CLI writer, so it discriminates nothing; `actor_id` names the kanban USER, and every agent writes through the ONE writeback user, so it cannot answer *which seat filed this*. The tag is the only per-seat provenance a card carries. **The compare is CASE-SENSITIVE**, deliberately the narrow direction: agent names are filesystem-cased config names, so `me` and `ME` can be two seats and a casefolded compare would let one correct the other's cards. Nothing is lost by being narrower than the writer.

- **⚑ Decision 2 — the caller-supplied id is established BOARD-SCOPED before anything reads or writes the card, reusing DL-323's primitive.** `card_id` reaches this tool as a literal a seat typed, against a kanban id space that is GLOBAL across every board on the instance — the same shape card#8375 closed on the writeback. The tool therefore resolves the card through `KanbanClient::cardRowsOnBoard($cfg->boardId, $cardId)` and **never calls `getCard()`**, whose own docblock now records that a caller reaching it with an author-supplied id and no such check is that defect rather than a shortcut. The verdict is read off the **rows** (own `id` names the card AND own `board_id` is the configured board), never off the call: the endpoint drops an unrecognised term to free text and still answers 200. Board scope and the mint stamp are two INDEPENDENT narrowings and both are required — neither is sufficient.

- **⛔ Decision 3 — the LANE is deliberately NOT part of the authorization.** A human may re-lane a card legitimately, and the mint stamp is what says the card is the seat's; a lane test would make a re-laned card permanently uncorrectable by the seat that filed it, with no other surface able to fix it. The response reports no lane and no lane flag as a consequence — **it reports only what was checked**, which is the DL-299/DL-302 rule (a value the tool did not read is never dressed as one it did) applied by omission rather than by a flag.

- **⭐ Decision 4 — the correction authority is NARROWER than `kbcard patch`'s corrective setters, and the rule is: this tool never writes a field `board_create_card` would refuse at birth.** The ruling that authorized the work enumerated `name, description, tags, type, external-id, origin` minus the bridge-owned (stage, DL stamps, pr fields). `type`, `external_id` and `origin` are **also refused**, because a correction authority WIDER than the create authority is a laundering route: mint a clean card, then "correct" in the reserved `type:` key, the `triaged` tag, or a payload key the create tool rejects outright — and the create guards would have been routed around rather than enforced. What is offered is `name` / `description` / `tags`: the caller-owned content, which is the motivating set the card named.

- **⚑ Decision 5 — a field this tool does not own is REFUSED BY NAME with its owner, never ignored.** `board_create_card` can ignore an out-of-scope argument (`swimlane_id: 999`) because its answer — *your card was created* — stays true. A correction that ignored one would answer 200 for a change it never made, which is the card's own acceptance criterion (*refuse loudly, never silently no-op*). Every plausible field carries its owner in the refusal (column moves are a different authority; the writeback owns payload/correlation refs; `external_id` is the board-unique sync id the bridge does not set even at create; `block_reason` is DL-193's; a retire is a lifecycle act), and anything else is refused as an unknown argument naming the accepted set.

- **⚠ Decision 6 — the tag write re-sends every tag on the card that is SOMEBODY ELSE'S CONTROL, and that PRESERVE set is a strict SUPERSET of the REFUSE set — not its read direction.** kanban replaces `tags` WHOLESALE, so a tag not re-sent is a tag deleted. ⛔ **THE FIRST CUT DERIVED PRESERVE FROM REFUSE AND CALLED THEM ONE RULE READ TWO WAYS. THEY ARE NOT, AND THE DERIVED SET IS THE SMALLER ONE.** Refuse answers *what may a caller not forge*; preserve answers *what on this card is somebody else's*. `no-automove` — `PinGuard`'s all-outcome writeback hold — is **forgeable on purpose** (a seat pinning its own card is legitimate, and `board_create_card` has always accepted the tag), so it is absent from the refuse vocabulary; deriving preserve from that vocabulary made a `tags` correction **delete a human's pin**, handing the next `merged` event the terminal move card#8289 exists to prevent. The tool refuses `block_reason` by name — the other half of the same pin — so the derived version protected one half and destroyed the other. **PRESERVE ⊇ REFUSE is the invariant**, and it now has two named members beyond the refuse set: `no-automove`, and **every `hold_marker_tags` value (DL-194) the install declares for the card's board**. What the caller cannot restore is the reason the reserved half is preserved (`created-by:` locks the seat out of its own card, `idem:` re-opens duplicate minting, `triaged`/`type:` undo the triage pass); what a HUMAN put there deliberately is the reason the hold half is.

- **⚑ Decision 6a — the operator-declared hold vocabulary IS reachable from a board-tools seat, through a board-keyed read that had to be added.** `hold_marker_tags` is declared per REPO mapping in `writeback.json`; a seat knows only `board_tools.board_id`. New primitive `WritebackConfig::holdMarkerTagsForBoard(int $boardId)` — the board-keyed, deduped read (several repo mappings can name one board, the same dedup `StandupService`'s Now-lane map makes) — sitting beside `boardIsShared()`, which is the same board-keyed question over the same array. The tool reads it through `WritebackConfig::loadDefault()`, which the board-tools path does NOT otherwise touch (`WritebackClientFactory` never loads `writeback.json`), so the three states are three different answers and are not collapsed: **absent file ⇒ `[]` is TRUE** (this install declares no hold tags), **parsed ⇒ the declared set**, **⛔ will not parse ⇒ the hold vocabulary is UNKNOWN and a `tags` correction is REFUSED** naming the file as an install fault — a wholesale replace under an unknown hold vocabulary is exactly the deletion this decision exists to stop. `name`/`description` corrections are unaffected: they write no tag list. Because the hold set is resolved BEFORE the ownership lookup, a call that cannot establish it reads nothing and writes nothing.

- **⛔ Decision 6b — the SIBLING AUDIT, with its bound.** Every tag any bridge code READS on a card was enumerated (`in_array`/`str_starts_with` over a card's `tags` across `app/Bridge`), not just the ones this tool knew about: `PinGuard::isPinned` (`no-automove`), `KanbanMoveCardHandler::shouldAlertUnpark` (`no-automove` + `hold_marker_tags`), `CoordinationClassifier` (`triaged`, `id:pr:` — both already reserved), and `KanbanCoordCardHandler` (`coord:reroute-archived`). **Two are out of reach rather than preserved, and the reason is structural, not an omission:** `coord:reroute-archived` and the `address_tags` a coord card must carry live on cards on `coord_board_id`, and a coord card carries no `created-by:<agent>` stamp — so `ownedRow()` refuses such a card before any tag list is composed. If this tool ever gained a coord-board write path, that pair joins the preserve set on the same day. The `dependencies` tag the dependabot handler writes is written and never read, and those cards carry no mint stamp either. ⚠ **The read-merge-write hazard `kbcard` records** — an unreadable tag list treated as "no tags" destroys every tag — stays UNREACHABLE rather than guarded: the preserved set is built from the SAME row whose tags had to contain `created-by:<agent>` for the call to be authorized, so a row with no readable tag list is refused before any write is composed.

- **⭐ Decision 7 — ONE argument rule: a PRESENT key is a correction, an ABSENT key leaves its field alone; and `null` and `""` are ONE VALUE, which is a MEASURED property of the door rather than a choice.** Laravel's global middleware stack carries `TrimStrings` and `ConvertEmptyStringsToNull` (read off the kernel, not assumed), so `"description": ""` is rewritten to `null` before `AgentToolsController` reads `args` — while the ssh door (`bridge:tools-call`) `json_decode`s the body itself and preserves it. Discriminating them would give one call two meanings depending on how the seat is wired; collapsing them keeps the contract transport-identical. So `description` present-and-empty CLEARS, `tags: []` means *drop my tags* (not *leave them alone*), and `name` has no clear form at all — a card cannot be left without one. ⛔ **AND THE DESCRIPTION IS TRIMMED, WHICH IS WHAT ACTUALLY MAKES "CLEAR" ONE VALUE ON BOTH DOORS.** The first cut collapsed `null`/`""` and stopped there, leaving `"   "` — three spaces — clearing on HTTP (`TrimStrings` runs ahead of `ConvertEmptyStringsToNull`) and writing whitespace over ssh: the same call, two meanings, which is the exact divergence this decision exists to close. `trim()` in `textCorrections()` converges them on the behaviour the HTTP door already had. ⚠ Measured on the SSH DOOR, because an HTTP-door test of `"   "` is vacuous — the middleware collapses the value before the tool sees it, so it passes against a tool that trims and one that does not. ⚠ **`board_create_card`'s opposite rule (a present `null` reads as ABSENT) is deliberately not copied and the divergence is recorded here rather than left to look like drift:** at birth there is nothing to clear, so `null` there cannot mean what it means here.

- **⚑ Decision 8 — a 4xx the BOARD answers is reported as a refusal (422), not as the retryable 502, and the predicate is DETERMINISM.** The dispatcher maps `RequestException` → 502 *"may be retryable"*, which is right for a 5xx and wrong for a request that fails identically however many times it is sent — answering "retry" to a permanent failure is the DL-020 storm shape. ⛔ **The first cut narrowed the arms to `{403, 404}` while stating determinism as the rule, and the gap was live in both directions:** a **401** (kanban v3 is `auth:sanctum`; a revoked or rotated writeback token) and a **422** (kanban's own validator rejecting a value) are as permanent as either, and both were reported as retryable. The arms are now **`{401, 403, 404}` on the lookup and `{401, 403, 404, 422}` on the write**, each naming its own cause, with the install-fault ones saying so. ⛔ **The 422 arm does not echo the board's response body** — it is an upstream artefact whose shape the bridge does not control; the refusal states the bridge's own bounded message instead. **The narrowing is still pinned by a control**: a 503 on the lookup and a 500 on the write both still answer 502.

- **⛔ Decision 8a — a REFUSAL MUST NAME A CAUSE THAT CAN PRODUCE IT, and the 403-on-lookup message did not.** It sent the operator to audit *"the writeback token's membership of your board"*, which kanban's search **never** answers 403 for: `TasksController::search` floors every caller to `Board::visibleTo($user)` and returns **200 with zero rows** for a board the token is not a member of. So the membership cause produces a NOT-FOUND, and it now says so where that lands — the not-yours refusal names it, mirroring DL-323's `mapped_board_unreadable_to_this_token` ("an unreadable board and an empty one are one answer here"). What does answer 403 on that route is kanban's per-token ABILITY gate (its DL-055: a GET needs `read`), and that is what the message names. ⚠ The membership sentence is on the **shared** message, deliberately: added to the no-rows arm alone it would make Decision 9's three arms distinguishable and turn the refusal into a card-existence oracle. A test asserts the two arms answer **byte-identically**.

- **⚑ Decision 8b — the bridge MIRRORS two of kanban's value rules, in ONE place, and states that it is a mirror.** `name => string|max:255` and `tags.* => string|max:64` (kanban's `App\Support\TaskWriteRules`) are now bounded bridge-side in `App\Bridge\Writeback\KanbanFieldLimits` and refused BY NAME before the request. Unbounded, a 256-character title reached the board, came back 422, and — under the first cut of Decision 8 — was reported as `502 upstream board error`: a seat retrying forever with no diagnosis. ⚠ **A mirror of a rule that lives in another repo can only be right until that repo moves it**, so it is a DIAGNOSTIC and never the safety: kanban's 422 is the safety, and Decision 8's 422 arm is what makes a stale mirror degrade the MESSAGE rather than the outcome. The seam is declared where the seam is documented (`docs/kanban-integration-contract.md`'s PATCH row), not only in the code. ⚠ **This is the one place the change is not additive:** the tag cap lives in the SHARED `CallerTagPolicy`, so `board_create_card` refuses an over-long tag too — see the accept/reject section.

- **⛔ Decision 9 — a not-yours refusal and a no-such-card refusal are ONE message, but an ARCHIVED card the caller OWNS is named.** The seat is never told whether a card it does not own exists — the same non-disclosure posture the door already takes on an unknown bearer (card#5778). The one exception is a card carrying the caller's own stamp on the archived side: the stamp proves the card is the caller's, so naming the retire discloses nothing, and the alternative is a guard telling a seat that a card it demonstrably filed "is not one of yours", which is a false statement. The archive probe reads the other side of kanban's archive SWITCH (DL-296, no both-sides mode) and runs **only when the live lookup misses**, so a successful call pays nothing for it.

- **⚑ Decision 10 — ONE general patch primitive on the client, and the three existing field writes are expressed in it.** `KanbanClient::patchCard(int $cardId, array $fields)` sends the flat `PATCH /tasks/{id}.json` body (kanban DL-219 dropped the `{"task":{…}}` wrapper); `moveCard`, `setBlockReason` and `stampCorrelationRefs` now delegate to it, wire-identical. Three byte-identical `->patch("/tasks/{$cardId}.json", […])->throw()` bodies were the primitive waiting to be named (the second-caller rule), and a fourth sibling was the alternative. It is a **thin verb that authorizes nothing** — which fields a caller may write, and whether it may write this card at all, is established by the caller before it is called; a guard inside the client would sit where it cannot see the authority. `archiveCard()` deliberately does NOT route through it (a top-level `_action` control key, and it reads its own response). ⭐ **This is the primitive a name restamp uses too** — card#8377 is landing one on a parallel branch, and both converge on this method rather than minting two.

- **⚠ ACCEPT/REJECT — what changes.** **Newly ACCEPTED:** a `board_correct_card` call from a seat with an enabled `board_tools` block, writing `name`/`description`/`tags` on a card carrying that seat's own `created-by:` stamp on that seat's configured board. **Nothing else is newly accepted**, and the two existing tools are byte-identical (`BoardCreateCardTool`'s only change is that its tag guard moved to a shared owner, with the same messages). An install that never enables board tools is unaffected — the registry is inert without a per-agent block, as DL-217 established. **Newly REFUSED — one case, and it is on the EXISTING tool:** `board_create_card` now refuses a tag longer than **64 characters** (Decision 8b's shared cap). It is not a new prohibition so much as a relocated one — kanban already 422'd that create, and the bridge reported it as a retryable `502 upstream board error` — but the door's answer changes from 502 to 422, so a consumer keying on the status sees it. Nothing else is newly refused, and `BoardCreateCardTool`'s other messages are byte-identical (its reserved-tag text is now pinned by a test after the extraction reworded it once).

- **Alternatives considered:**
  - **Offer the full `kbcard patch` setter set.** Rejected — Decision 4: it makes the correction tool a route around the create tool's guards, and the fields dropped are exactly the ones create refuses.
  - **Scope on `actor_id` / `actor_type` from `last_stage_move`.** Rejected on the card's own evidence: `service` covers every CLI writer and `actor_id` names the shared writeback user. Neither identifies a seat.
  - **Also require the card to be in the seat's own swimlane.** Rejected — Decision 3: a legitimate re-lane would make the card permanently uncorrectable, and the mint stamp is the authorization the rule is stated in.
  - **Replace the tag list verbatim, as `kbcard --tags` does for a human.** Rejected — Decision 6. `kbcard`'s caller can re-supply a reserved tag; this one cannot, by construction.
  - **A wholesale `board_patch_card` taking a field map.** Rejected: the authority is the point of this tool, and a field map is an allow-list wearing a general interface. The refusal table IS the contract.
  - **Let 403/404 fall through to the dispatcher's 502.** Rejected — Decision 8: it tells a seat to retry a request that can never succeed, and hides the one diagnosis the operator needs.
  - **Read the card back after the write to echo its resulting state.** Rejected as unpriced mechanism: the response reports the fields it SENT (`tags_written` is named for that), and `board_my_cards` is one call away. `board_create_card` pays a read-back because a POST hands back an id and nothing else; a PATCH answers about a card the caller already named.

- **Consequences:** new `app/Bridge/Tools/BoardCorrectCardTool.php`; new `app/Bridge/Tools/CallerTagPolicy.php` (the reserved vocabulary + sanitizer, extracted from `BoardCreateCardTool` at its second caller, plus the separate `isPreserved()` direction — there is no `isReserved()`, which the first cut had and Decision 6 replaced); new `app/Bridge/Writeback/KanbanFieldLimits.php` (Decision 8b's mirrored caps, one owner); `app/Bridge/Writeback/WritebackConfig.php` (+`holdMarkerTagsForBoard()`, Decision 6a); `app/Bridge/Support/BoardToolsConfig.php` (its docblock enumerated the tool set and now points at `BoardToolsRegistry`); `app/Bridge/Tools/BoardCreateCardTool.php` (delegates its tag guard, keeps ownership of WHY each entry is reserved); `app/Bridge/Tools/BoardToolsRegistry.php` (three tools). `app/Bridge/Writeback/KanbanClient.php` (+`patchCard`; `moveCard`/`setBlockReason`/`stampCorrelationRefs` delegate, and the DL-219 flat-body / payload-merge notes de-duplicate onto the primitive). Tests: new legs in `tests/Feature/AgentTools/AgentToolsCallTest.php` (the refusal table, the preserve set, the value bounds, the four board-answered statuses, the non-disclosure identity) and 2 in `tests/Feature/Writeback/KanbanClientTest.php`; one on the SSH door (`ToolsCallCommandTest`) for the cross-door clear, which is the only door that can measure it; and new `tests/Feature/AgentTools/ChannelServerToolSurfaceRestatementTest.php` — the drift GUARD for the tag vocabulary and the caps the channel server's inline MCP schema restates (DELETE is unavailable there: a `tools/list` description IS the surface a model reads, with no pointer it can follow, so canon #16's other arm applies). **Every guard was watched RED against a mutant**, the drift guard against a GROWN constant rather than an edited string; plus the census repair below. ⛔ **THE CONSOLIDATION SILENTLY NARROWED ANOTHER GUARD'S POPULATION, AND THAT GUARD CAUGHT IT** — recorded because it is the more valuable half of this change. `WritebackSuccessBoardRecordTest` derives the client's WRITE methods by scanning `KanbanClient` for a method whose body issues `->patch(`/`->post(`/`->delete(`; the instant `moveCard` / `setBlockReason` / `stampCorrelationRefs` delegated to `patchCard`, those three stopped matching and **nine accounted call sites left the card#7212 census while every behavioural test stayed green**. The derivation now follows `$this-><method>(` to a FIXED POINT, so it describes what a write IS rather than how one is spelled today, with a control fixture that is positive and negative in one (a method delegating to a READ must not be a writer) and was watched red against a no-transitive-leg mutant. A correct consolidation narrowing the population a guard derives over is the general shape; this is the instance (stamp check removed; stamp compare casefolded; row `board_id` unchecked; reserved tags not preserved; foreign arguments ignored; archive probe removed; the two 403/404 mappings collapsed to 502; an empty tag list read as an omission). Docs: `docs/board-tools.md` (a full section + the tool table, the discovery line, the 422 row, and a sentence reconciling DL-304's fallback-retirement derivation with a SECOND responder that emits `board_id` — the condition survives because `BoardToolsScopeHeader::read()`'s only two callers both send the literal `board_my_cards`, so this tool's envelope cannot reach the legacy fallback), `docs/writeback.md` (its statement of how the write census derives the client's write VERBS was falsified by the `patchCard` delegation — the three narrow verbs no longer issue `->patch(` themselves — and now states the transitive rule), `docs/kanban-integration-contract.md` (the PATCH row — see below), `CLAUDE.md` (the doc-index row), `examples/channel-servers/agent-webhook-bridge-channel.mjs` + `package.json`/`package-lock.json` (**0.9.8 → 0.9.9**) + its README, `docs/CHANGELOG.md`. **Three more surfaces ENUMERATE the tool set and were completed rather than left partly true** — `docs/config-schema.md`'s `board_tools:` heading, `docs/multi-host.md`'s forward-leg section and `docs/writeback.md`'s opening paragraph — found by grepping the tool NAME across the docs rather than by grepping the file this change touched; the frozen release rows in `CLAUDE.md` and the historical DL entries are deliberately not edited.

- **⚠ A STALE CONTRACT ROW WAS CORRECTED IN PASSING, and it was stale before this change.** `docs/kanban-integration-contract.md`'s `PATCH /api/v3/tasks/{id}.json` row said the bridge uses that endpoint to *"Move a card"* with body *"`{workflow_stage_id}` **only**"* — untrue since DL-193 (`block_reason`) and the correlation-ref payload delta, both of which PATCH the same endpoint. It now names every field write the bridge makes, the one client primitive that constructs them, and the two OPPOSITE field semantics (`payload` merges per key; `tags` is replaced wholesale). §3's `Move = workflow_stage_id-only PATCH` invariant is about the MOVE and is unchanged — the two rows are stated so they cannot read as contradicting.

- **Bounds, stated.** **NOT MEASURED AGAINST A LIVE KANBAN.** That `name`/`description`/`tags` are writable as flat fields on `PATCH /tasks/{id}.json` is **source-verified twice over** — kanban's create body takes all three as top-level fillable fields, and the toolkit's shipped `kbcard patch` writes exactly that flat body against the same v3 endpoint — but no request from this branch has been made against a running instance. The failure direction if it is wrong is a non-2xx, i.e. a loud refusal, never a silent partial write. **The `tags`-replaced-wholesale semantic comes from the same source** (`kbcard`'s `_kbc_patch_tags` read-merge-writes precisely because of it) and is what Decision 6 is built on; if kanban ever merged tags instead, the preservation would be redundant rather than wrong. **A PRE-EXISTING CROSS-DOOR ASYMMETRY IS DISCLOSED, AND IS NOW NARROWER THAN IT WAS:** `TrimStrings` runs on the HTTP door and not on the ssh one, so a value with surrounding whitespace is trimmed on one transport and stored verbatim on the other. It predates this change (`board_create_card`'s `title` has the same asymmetry) and it remains for **`name`/`title`**, where it is cosmetic — the bytes differ, the meaning does not. It is GONE for `description`, where it was not cosmetic: Decision 7's `trim()` is what removes the case where the same call MEANT two different things (clear vs write whitespace), which the first cut of this entry claimed without having done. **⚠ TWO SIBLINGS OF DECISION 8/8b ARE NAMED AND LEFT OPEN, deliberately, because closing either changes what an EXISTING tool accepts or answers and that is the operator's call, not this card's** (canon: report the shape, do not widen the scope on momentum). **(1)** `board_create_card`'s `title` is still unbounded, so an over-long title is still a kanban 422 reported as a retryable `502 upstream board error` — the same defect the correction tool's `name` cap closes, on the tool next to it. It is one line and `KanbanFieldLimits::NAME_MAX` already exists. **(2)** the board-answered 401/403/404/422 → refusal mapping is `board_correct_card`'s alone; `board_my_cards` and `board_create_card` still send every board 4xx to the dispatcher's retryable 502, so a rotated writeback token puts a seat in the same retry loop through either of them. Both are recommended, neither is done here. *[Additive annotation, 2026-09-02 (card#8486, DL-339): BOTH ARE NOW DONE, on the operator ruling this sentence asks for. The mapping was HOISTED into `App\Bridge\Tools\BoardCallRefusal` rather than copied, `board_create_card` and `board_my_cards` migrated, and `title` bounded at `NAME_MAX`; `board_correct_card`'s own answers are byte-for-byte unchanged except its write-403, which DL-339 Decision 8 corrects — it named two of the gates kanban can refuse a write with and not the third. The sentence stands as written, per this log's frozen-original convention (DL-277) — nothing it decides moves, and its reading of the two instances is what DL-339 implements.]* **THE OWNERSHIP RULE IS ONLY AS GOOD AS THE STAMP:** a card the seat filed through any other route — the PM, `kbcard`, the coord reconcile — carries no `created-by:` tag and is not correctable by this tool, by design; and an agent RENAMED in config loses the ability to correct its earlier cards, which is the price of keying on the name the stamp carries.
